So, what are the important phases in the application development lifecycle is the testing phase. Now there are several types of testing. The first line of defense when testing code is called unit testing, which is typically performed by the developer or development team. Now when working with Java, a unit usually refers to a method. Now a developer could run tests on his or her code manually. For example, if we wanted to test a method that performs a calculation, and displays the result to the user, we could manually run the method with a set of test values, and verify that we get the expected result back.

But that's tedious. And what would happen when we made changes to the method, we'd have to run the tests all over again, and perhaps add even more test values. Now, instead of running tests manually, developers can use a unit testing framework to write tests that will run in an automated fashion. When working on a team that's coding a large application, the build process for the application will typically run a unit test suite after each successful build.

And if 100% of the tests are successful, that's great. But if not, then the failed tests will tell the developers what recent changes to the code may have broken a part of the application. For smaller applications with a single developer, the developer can still run the test suite after changing any code. The J unit is a popular testing framework that we can use to run unit tests. LECTURE 25.3: JavaFX Fundamentals: MVC, Application Lifecycle, and Stages
----------------------------------------

All right. So at the stage, now we've created our first project, we've configured it to work with either JDK 8 or JDK 11. So let's start talking more about javafx. So javafx was designed with the MVC or model view controller pattern in mind. In a nutshell, this pattern keeps the code that handles an application's data separate from the UI code. Because of this, when you're using the MVC pattern, we shouldn't mix the code that deals with the ui and the code that manipulates the application data in the same class.

The controller is sort of a middleman between the UI and the data. Now when working with javafx, the model corresponds to the application's data model, the view is the fxml and the controller is the code that determines what happens when a user interacts with the ui. Essentially, the controller handles events, which we'll cover in a later video. Now that's a bit of a simplification of the MVC pattern, but it's enough for us to understand why intellij generates a controller.java file for us.

If I open up the project, you can see we've got a controller, a main and sample.fxml as well. I'm going to close down the module info.java because we won't be needing that anymore. And just to note to keep in mind that javafx doesn't actually enforce the MVC pattern, but it is a good practice to follow. So for this simple hello world application that we are going to generate, there isn't any data. Also, the code generated by intellij doesn't create any javafx UI controls.

Apart from the usual windows controls to minimize, maximize and close, there's nothing to interact with. And so therefore, if we have a look at the controller.java file, it's actually empty. But going back to the main.java file, the structure should look familiar because it is still a java class just like any other. Firstly, though on line 9, we can see that the class extends application. An application actually comes from javafx.application. Javafx applications must have a class that extends this application class.

And this class will be the entry point for the application. The application class manages the life cycle of a javafx application. The methods in the application class that we really care most about are the init method, the start method and the stop method. When we run the application, application.launch will be called from the main method. This method launches the javafx application and doesn't return until the application has exited. When a javafx application is launched, the init method runs first.

In the application class, this method is empty, so unless we override it it won't do anything. The start method runs right after the init method. We have to override this class because start is an abstract method in the application class. We create the UI in the start method as you'll see in a moment. Now when the application finishes, which usually happens because the users close the application's main window, the stop method runs. Just like the init method, this method is empty in the application class.

So unless we override it, it won't do anything. So to start off though, let's start looking at this start method that intellij generated starting on line 12. This method takes a stage parameter, as you can see. So a stage is a top-level javafx container that extends the window class. So essentially, it's the main window. The javafx runtime constructs the initial stage and passes it into the start method. We can create other stages, but most applications will only have one top level window, too many windows can lead to a bad user experience.

In this version of javafx, dialogues are presented within a stage, but we don't explicitly create the stage. We use the dialogue class which wraps the dialogue into a stage for us. The javafx developers have said that in a future version of javafx, they may provide a lightweight container for dialogues rather than using a stage. So note that the dialogue class was introduced in java version 8u40. Before then, creating dialogues was a real pain. So we'll probably use the dialogue class at some point.

But if anyone's got a problem compiling classes that reference dialogue, most likely it'll be because they're using a JDK version earlier than supported the dialogue class which was again version 8. But these days if you're using JDK 11 you really shouldn't have any problems. All right. So that's the first line talking about the method signature, the parameter stage. The next line of code, line 13, that loads the UI from the fxml file. So it's probably a good opportunity now to have a look at this fxml file.

This is the sample.fxml file. So fxml is a flavor of xml. If you're familiar with the android UI programming, fxml will be old hat to you. But in this particular application this default one all we have is a grid pane, which is one of the javafx layouts. The fx colon controller attribute tells the runtime, which class is the controller for this window. You can see that it's package name and dot class name. So sample being the package name controller being our controller class.

The grid pane doesn't have any child elements. And so when we run the application. As you saw in a previous video, the window is going to be empty, and it's empty here now. Now depending on your version of the JDK, you'll find that there's probably a few leftover imports that aren't used. For some reason they're generated with those unnecessary imports. Right now we only need the grid pane import, but later on we'll be using a label as well. But I'll leave them there for now, but you could actually delete them if you wanted to.

So going back to main.java, when we load the fxml file, which we do on line 13, all of the UI objects defined in the file are constructed. So we'll come back to the parent root part of the code in a moment. But go moving on to line 14, we set the title of the stage. Since the window class is the parent of the stage class and as we learned previously the stage is the top level javafx container, this essentially means that the window title will be set to in this case hello world.

On line 15, we're setting the stages scene. If you haven't already guessed, the javafx developers were going for a theatre metaphor. Each stage requires a scene and backing each scene is a scene graph a tree in which each node corresponds to a UI control or an area of the scene for example a rectangle. So let's take a look at this line, line 15 in more detail. When we loaded the fxml, we assign it to a variable of type parent with the name root.

The parent class descends directly from the node class, which is -- and taking this from the javadoc the base class for scene graph nodes. Notes that descend from parent can have children in the scene graph. Now for the hello world application, the top level and in fact only node is the grid pane. So the grid paint node will be the root of the scene graph. And that's what was returned from the fxml loader.load call on line 13. When we construct a scene, we have to pass in the root of the scene graph that will back the scene, which we do here.

We're also setting the width and height of the scene which in turn will become the width and height of the main window. So why do we have to have a scene at a stage. Well, let's go back to the theater metaphor and imagine that you're watching a play. The curtain rises when we watch the first scene, then the curtain falls stagehands run around and change the furniture and backdrop and then the curtain rises again. We may see a different looking set of different actors, but it's still the same stage.

So if you go back to javafx, remember that a stage corresponds to a top level UI container, like a window and a scene is backed by a c graph which contains the UI nodes. If you want to change what's shown in a stage, the window, all we have to do is change the scene, the UI. We don't have to construct a new stage object. In practice, we would load a different fxml file into a new scene and then called stage.setscene. For example, if we had a wizard that we wanted the user to step through using next and previous buttons, we could use the same window stage and just change the scene every time they clicked next or previous or when we wanted to change parts of the UI in response to a user action, we don't have to remove ui components or make them invisible and add new ones, we just switch the scene.

Sometimes it makes more sense to just hide a few controls or something like that, but other times switching the entire scene is the better option. It will depend on what you want to do. Essentially, those scenes make it easy to reuse a container. All right, so back to our main java class. At this point we've instantiated all the UI objects associated with our scene. And we've set the stage so we're ready now to show the UI. And we do this by calling the show method on our stage, and we're doing that on line 16.

From the code and the fxml file, we know that when we run the application, we should see an empty window with the title hello world. So we'll just run the application again and confirm that. No surprises, empty window, and we can see hello world as a title at the top of the window. So as you can see the stage class provides all the window decorations, such as clothes, resize and the minimize button. All right, so that's a bit of an overview of how javafx works.

Let's finish the video here. And in the next one, we're going to start making some modifications to our application. We're going to change the title and look at how to code some of this stuff manually as opposed to getting it done automatically for us. So we'll see you in the next video.

Okay, so moving on we're now going to talk about layouts. Now with JavaFX, layouts allow us to add controls which are ui components to a container without having to write the code required to manage the positioning and also the resizing behavior of those controls. Now the layout will manage all of that for us which is pretty cool. So JavaFX has got 8 layouts. And you don't need to memorize this, but the 8 layouts are called the GridPane, the AnchorPane, StackPane, hbox, vbox, FlowPane, TilePane and also the BorderPane.

Now before we get into playing with layouts, I just want to discuss what I mean by the preferred size for JavaFX controls. Because preferred size is actually an important concept. So every control computes its preferred size based on its contents. So what I'm talking about preferred size what I mean is the preferred width and height of the control when it's displayed. As an example JavaFX has got a button control, now we're obviously familiar with buttons, especially ones for okay and cancer which you've seen in applications in the past.

By default, the button control will size itself so there's enough room to display its content whatever's actually in there, the text in other words. So if we were working with an ok button, the button control would size itself so that its border fits around that text okay in this example. So it wouldn't stretch itself across the width of the entire window for example it would only be just wide enough to accept that text. So layouts often use the preferred size of the controls they're laying out to determine how much space a controller will ultimately get.

So when a controller is placed into a layout, it becomes a child of that layout. So some layouts will ensure that their children display at their preferred widths or heights. And sometimes it will depend on where control is placed within the layout. So that's the theory. Let's actually get started and go through what some of this actually looks like in code. Now before we do, we have to talk about the concept of a procedural driven program versus an event driven program. So console applications that we've used primarily in this course prior to this section or other ones that don't have a user interface are procedural driven.

So in other words, they run from the entry point of the application to the last line of the code. So there may be conditional statements that influence exactly which code is executed, but when the application runs, we'll know roughly in what order each method and line of code will actually be executed. But ui applications are event driven. And that's because the user dictates what code will be run and when and that's by clicking on particular controls on the screen.

So to use that analogy, let's think about intellij again. So when we run intellij it doesn't run its code from beginning to end and then stop executing. The window remains up, and the application has no idea what the user i.e. us the programmers want to do with it. So one user might start by creating a new file, but another user might open the settings dialog someone else might create a new project and go to help, then rearrange the layout of the main window perhaps.

So intellij will only close or stop executing when the user tells it to by closing the main window or of course by going to file and selecting exit which no doubt you've done a number of times before. So typically the life cycle of a ui program is as follows. You'll run the initialization code, it will then build the main user interface and then then wait for user input. When the user does something like for example pressing a button or typing something into a field or perhaps selecting a menu item, the application will run the code that handles that particular event based on what the user has actually done what they've clicked or what they've been interacted with with the control on the screen. So in other words, it's going to run the event handler for that particular event.

When the user closes the main window or indicates that you know in some other way that they'd like to exit the application any cleanup code will run and the application will then exit at that point. So in this lecture we're interested in that part of the cycle where the application is waiting for user input. So in javafx, the javafx application thread also known as the ui thread waits for user input. So later on we'll come back to this thread. And actually in a later section of the course, we're going to be going into threads in more detail.

But for now let's just go back to this example that we've knocked up our say hello button. So when the user presses a button or interacts with any type of control, an event is actually raised on the ui thread. So in other words, the ui thread notices that the user's done something then check to see if any part of the application has expressed interest in handling whatever the user has done for that or interacted with for that particular control.

So if it finds something, it's going to run the event handler the application has associated with that event. In our case, what we'd like to do is we'd like to run an event handler when the user presses the say hello button. So our first step is to write the event handler. So what's going on here what does that actually mean. Well, it turns out that the scene graph isn't thread safe. So in other words, the code assumes that nodes in the screen graph will only ever be updated by the same thread namely the UI thread and which we've learned is also known as the java fx application thread. So if more than one thread could update a node, it would be possible for the internal integrity of the node to be compromised if you think about it.

So for example if thread a runs and starts to change the state of a node and then it's suspended so that thread b can run, nothing in the java fx code prevents thread b from also updating the same node. So in other words, thread b could wipe out, what thread a had started, so there'd be some sort of compromise there's two processes on the computer running at the same time and they're sort of conflicting with each other. So basically thread b could wipe out what 3 has started as I mentioned.

And when thread a runs again it continues its updates not knowing that its previous updates were overwritten by thread b. So you can see how the internal state or integrity of a node could be compromised in that situation. Now because of that the developers of java fx were keenly aware that this has been a problem and so whenever we want to work with nodes on the scene graph, we actually must do so on the javafx application thread. Now if we don't, in other words if we try to update something as I've done here that's not in the UI thread, then we're going to actually get an exception like this one, which was of course was the illegal state exception.

And again, in our code we're trying to update the label you can see that on line 41. So as although this is an error at least javafx is actually stopping us from doing it, knowing that down the track could be you'd be getting all sorts of problems with your code anyway. But anyway enough about the theory how do we actually fix this. Well, when we're doing a long task on a background thread, we usually want to update a part of the UI when the task is finished. And we'll also select the new item so that the user can see the details and deadline they just entered on screen. Now before java 8 u40, there wasn't any support for dialogues.

And that really was a huge oversight on the part of javafx developers. Now they may have believed that developers were mainly going to use the javafx for web and mobile applications perhaps where dialogues don't really make as much sense, but that hasn't turned out to be the case and most desktop applications use dialogues. So to create a dialogue using earlier versions of javafx, even simple dialogs that just you know really display a confirmation message and an ok button.

To do that, we have to create a whole new window and take care of most of the background plumbing code ourselves. But fortunately, javafx 8u40 introduced a dialogue and DialoguePane classes and that makes creating dialogues a lot easier. At the same time javafx also added support for a bunch of common dialogue types. And we're going to use 1 of the can dialogue types later, but to start off we're going to create a custom dialogue for the add new to-do item case. Now if you're running a JDK earlier than java 8u40, you won't be able to use the dialogue and DialoguePane classes and you should really upgrade to the latest JDK version.

There isn't really a solid reason not to update. And just to check what version you are running, a couple of ways of doing it, but the simplest way is just to right click on the project name, come down here to open module settings and it should show you if you've got to module selected, it will show you on the module sdk project is SDK 8.1. And you can normally just open that up, and you can have a look at the version there you can see how. In this case, I've got 18.0 underscore 73.

So that is effectively sort of like 8u73. So you really want a number basically that's version 8 and greater than the number 40 to be able to use this. And again, as I said, there's no real reason not to update to the latest version of java 8, so I do suggest you do that. Now in terms of the dialogues UI, we can't create this in the same fxml file that we've used so far in our application for the main window, and that's because each fxml file can really only have 1 root node meaning ultimately 1 scene graph.

Now our dialogue will use a different scene graph from the main window. And so we'll have to create a new fxml file and then associate a separate controller with it as well. And unfortunately, there's no support in intellij to do this. So in other words, we really have to do this ourselves.So we're going to start by come over here to the package. And we're going to put it basically at the same level that we've got our fmxl file. And again, we can click in that we've got that on the screen there now.

And I'm just going to basically just click here in the package new file. We're going to call this 1 to do item dialogue.fxml. I'll just close down the run window. So every instance of the dialogue wraps a DialoguePane instance. So in other words, the DialoguePane is always the top level layout of a dialogue. And now if we go back to our to do item dialogue, the error disappears because the class now exists. So let's talk a little bit about how the DialoguePane works.

Now it's a layout manager that's used for dialogues as you can probably guess. And it allows us to set 4 properties, namely the header, graphic, content and buttons. Now each property expects a control. Because we often want to display text for the header and the content, the DialoguePane also has 2 convenience properties, header text and content text. And when we want the header or content to display a string using the convenience properties saves us from having to create a label property for the text.

If both the non-text property and the text property is set, then the non-text property will take precedence. For example, if we set the header property to a control and we also set the header text property, the header value will be used and then the header text value will be ignored. LECTURE 25.28: Data Binding Mastery: Implementing Observable Lists for Dynamic UI in JavaFX
----------------------------------------

So as I alluded to in the previous video, we're not going to change the way that we populate the ListView. And that's because the way that we've been doing it so far isn't really recommended. Now the way we've done it so far does work, but it's not the way we'd want to do it in a real world application. When we add to do items, what we're doing is we're explicitly updating the ListView by repopulating it again. Now not only is that inefficient but in a more complex application that's got many different ways for the user to change what our control is displaying, it would be really easy for the controller to get out of sync with the data, so we definitely don't want that to happen.

So instead of explicitly trying to manage what the ListView is displaying, we're going to use what's called data binding. Now when we bind a control to data or data, the control is going to notice when the data changes without us having to write any code. So the control will you know seemingly update itself. So if we scroll down and have a look, you can see here when we're loading the items the code on line 44 it's using fx collections.observable arraylist. You probably saw that previously, in previous videos when we created it and you might be wondering why we're using it.

And in fact why are we using an observable list from the javafx API rather than say using a general list from the java.util.collections package. Well, we're doing it for performance reasons. As we've learned observable lists will raise events and because methods within the list classes may call each other when a list is changed, it's then possible for more than one event to be raised for a single change. Now for example if method a b and c all raise events and when an item is added then method a calls b, which calls c then 3 events will be raised whenever an item's added.

And the UI operations can be expensive and that's because the UI control has to paint the screen or part of itself on the on the actual screen on the display. So we don't want to control like a ListView to run its handler multiple times when an item is added or deleted. Ideally, what we want is to only run with handler once. Now the fx collections package contains a copy of all the classes and static methods in the java.util.collections package, but the code has been optimized to reduce the number of events or notifications raised when the collections changed.

Now as it says in the fx clock collections documentation, which I'll bring up the link for shortly, all methods are optimized in a way that only yield limited numbers of notifications. On the other hand java.util.collections might call modification methods or an observable list multiple times resulting in a number of notifications. And I'll just bring up that documentation on the screen, suggest you go and check that out at your leisure.You can read more about this there's the link there top left hand corner.

Again, you can see here the utility methods here are mainly for performance reasons. And they're optimized in a way that only yield or that they yield only limited number of notifications. So the bottom line with all this, we're getting back to our code is that we really always want to use the fx collections versions, not the version in java.util collections. And that's why we've used this observable arraylist on line 44 to do that. So let's add an item. LECTURE 25.37: Leveraging SceneBuilder: A Visual Approach to JavaFX UI Design within IntelliJ

Okay. So we've learned how to create our UI using fxml. And we've been doing so by editing the fxml file. Now instead of writing the fxml ourselves, we could have used the javafx scene builder tool. Now scene builder is a GUI builder, graphical user interface builder. Now we can actually use it to build our user interface by dragging and dropping javafx controls and containers onto a content area. Scene builder then generates the fxml code for us.

And it's written using javafx, so it's an example of a complex javafx application. Now at this point you might be wondering why we've spent so much time learning how to code fxml when we could have really just used a tool like scene builder instead. Well, GUI builders can be wonderful tools that do make our life easier. But when using any tool that generates code, it's really important to learn how to write the code yourself first. And the reason for that is the tool might get discontinued, we might want to tweak the generated code or perhaps you need to debug the code when it doesn't work as you would expect.

Now GUI builders should always be seen as a way to help us create the user interface. They shouldn't ever be used because we don't actually know how to write the code ourselves so we don't understand what's happening behind the scenes. And that's why we've spent so many lessons in this section, learning the manual way of creating fxml, so the scene builder tool is going to really make things really going to complement our skills now that we've sort of started off on the manual way and we can now save a bit of time using scene builder.

Now when it does come to scene builder, the javafx community is wondering And I'm in the same boat here whether oracle and that's the company obviously that own java and everything related to it will actually keep the tool under active development. Now to give you an example of that, oracle used to offer installers for a scene builder, but they no longer do. Oracle instruct developers who want to use the tool to download the source code and to build the tool themselves.

And also oracle have made the scene builder code open source and potentially that could mean that oracle don't have any real sort of long-term plans to work on it anymore, pure speculation. But in any event fortunately, the javafx community has stepped up to the plate and they've actually kept the scene builder code in sync with javafx update, something that oracle haven't been doing, but of course that could change at any time. For now though the scene builder is still a tool we can use and it is still very useful.

Now if you search for scene builder, you might find some old binaries from oracle that you can use, but they don't actually include the latest updates to javafx. So what I'm going to do is in the next few videos, I'm going to actually show you how to find an alternative way to get scene builder installed on a windows machine and also on a mac machine and although I won't have a video for Linux users, I'll also outline how you can go about getting that for your platform.

SECTION 26: Deep Dive into the Java 9 Module System: JPMS Fundamentals
########################################

----------------------------------------
LECTURE 26.1: Comprehensive Introduction to Java Modules: Concepts, Goals, and Structure
----------------------------------------

All right. So let's talk about a brand new feature in java 9 modules. So one of the most important and exciting features of JDK 9 is the module system and that was developed under a project code name of jigsaw. Now java 9 introduced a new program component known as a module. So think of a java application as a collection of modules. Now the module system was designed to have a reliable configuration strong encapsulation and a modular JDK JRE. So the purpose is to solve the problems typically involved with developing and deploying java applications prior to java 9.

Now these modularity features in java 9 are collectively known as the java platform module system or JPMS. So what is a module? So module is a named collection of data and code. Now modules can contain java code that's organized as a set of packages. Now which package can contain classes interfaces and so on. So think ultimately of a module as a container of packages. Now each module needs to have some configuration, the name, the unique name of the module, inputs what the module needs to use and what is required for the module to be compiled and run as well as outputs. So what the module outputs or exports to other modules.

So doing it this way you don't have to specify every package that your module needs, only the name of a module you depend on. So more on this later though when we create our own first module in code. So the java SE9 platform is divided into a set of modules that are known as platform modules. Now this provides a scalable java runtime. The standard modules have names prefixed with java. For example, java.base java.sql and so on. And as an example in this course we've used javafx to create graphical user interfaces.

Now the javafx module names are prefixed with javafx. Let's see a diagram on the next slide that illustrates the input and output definitions of a module. So you can see the slide here, we've got inputs and we've also got outputs from a module. So we've got the module itself, the module definition, then we define the inputs for the modules as well as the exports which are packages. And then we go down to the module code, and we've got internal packages as well as exported packages.

So each module comes with a module descriptor file, and we'll talk more about the module descriptor file in this video. And as I mentioned, we have internal packages and also external packages and also exported packages which can obviously be exported that enables other modules to use those exported packages. All right. So every module comes with a module descriptor file that describes the module and contains metadata about the module. Now that module descriptor file is always located directly at the module root folder and always has the name module-info.java.

So let's see a minimalistic module descriptor example. So you can see it on the screen there, there's a new keyword introduced module and that's followed by the module name and curly braces. And in this example, you can see that I've used academy.learnprogramming.com as the module name. Now inside the curly braces, you can optionally add metadata about the module. In other words, inputs and outputs, but we'll talk more about that later in this section.

So a module declaration introduces a module name that can be used in other module declarations to express relationships between modules. So a module name consists of one or more java identifiers separated by the period or the dot tokens no different to how you declare a package, and the two kind of modules normal modules and open modules. Now the kind of a module determines access to the module's types and the members of those types for code outside the module.

So a normal module without the open modifier grants access at compile time and runtime to types in only those packages which are explicitly exported. Now an open module with the open modifier grants access at compile time to types in only those packages which are explicitly exported. However, it also grants access at run time to types in all its packages as if all packages had been exported. So let's see a project structure with and without modules.

You can see on the left-hand side, we've got a project structure as it would have looked before java 9. And on the right-hand side we've got a project structure with java 9.. Now before java 9 we had a source directory with packages that contained java files but with java 9. There's another directory the module root directory which will contain module info.java which we talked about as well as package directories. Now with java 9 modular programming, we don't have to build applications as one big java project we can create modular units that work together to form an application.

So modules are ideally components that are reusable that solve specific requirements for that app. So you can think of modules as high level packages keep in mind that they're actually not packages. All right. So in summary project jigsaw had the following primary goals to create a scalable platform and that's to give the ability to scale the platform down to smaller computing devices. And I achieved that by moving from a monolithic run time. The second goal was security and maintainability and to make a more maintainable platform code base that had better organization and also has its internal API hidden so that we've got better modular interfaces to improve platform security.

Third goal was improved application performance. So a platform that's smaller with only the necessary runtimes which then results in faster performance. And number four easier development experience. So as a result of the module system and the modular platform combination, it's made it easy for developers to create applications and libraries. All right. So let's move on to the next video. We're going to look at the module declaration and statements, so I'll see you in the next video.

----------------------------------------
LECTURE 26.2: Mastering Java Module Declarations and Statements: Requires, Exports, and Opens
----------------------------------------

All right. So module declaration and statements. So let's discuss now on modules declaration and statements that are used. So as I discussed in the previous video, each module is defined using a module declaration using the newly introduced module keyword. So the syntax is the following. So you can see we've got module, module name. We've got curly braces and then some module statements and closing curly brace. And optionally, we've got this open modifier.

Now the open modifier declares an open module or in other words a module that exports all its packages to be used by reflective access, but more on this later when we start creating modules. All right. So the module name is the name of the defined module. And the module name is mandatory. We can't have two modules inside the same code base with the same name. And it's good practice to name modules with the same name as packages. And inside the curly braces, we can have zero or more module statements.

And those statements can be the export statement the open statement, the requires statement, user statement or the provides statement. So the require statement is used to specify the module that's required by the current module. In other words, if our module depends on some other modules, we have to specify it using the requires statement. Now we can use multiple required statements depending on how many modules are needed for our module. Now the export statement is used to specify the packages that are exported by the current module. Now the provide statement is used to specify the service implementations that the current modules provide. Now the user statement is used to specify the service that the current module consumes.

And a final point here is keep in mind that the open statement can't be used in open modules because all packages are open in an open module. All right. So let's move on to the next video now we're going to discuss module types and the module path. So I'll see you in the next video.

----------------------------------------
LECTURE 26.3: Exploring Java Module Types: Named, Unnamed, Automatic, Open, and Aggregator
----------------------------------------

All right. Let's talk about the various module types in project jigsaw. So project jigsaw defines two types of modules namely named modules and unnamed modules. So let's see a breakdown of each type. So you can see that we've got named modules and unnamed modules. Now named modules can be automatic or normal modules. And still further we can break down normal modules which can be basic modules or open modules. So let's discuss some named modules in more detail.

So firstly, for named modules each named module has a name. Now named modules can be normal or automatic. Now name modules are modules declared in the module- info.java file which is the module descriptor file. So that's actually a requirement for named modules. And all platform modules are named modules. Now normal modules don't officially exist in the in JDK 9. We just use the term normal for a named module that isn't an automatic module. And again, a normal module has a module descriptor file.

In other words, the module-info.java file while an automatic module doesn't have a module descriptor file. And a normal module is declared using the keyword module. A normal module doesn't export any of its packages by default. And finally, a normal module is divided into basic and open modules. All right. So contrast that to automatic modules. So an automatic module is created after adding a jar file to the module path. Now unlike a named module, an automatic module is not explicitly declared by the developer inside the module descriptor.

Rather it's automatically created when a jar file is placed into the module path. Now it requires by default all platform modules, all our own modules and all other automatic modules. And by default, it exports all its packages. Now these are useful for third-party code, and we'll be talking more about that later, and they're also used for migrating existing applications to java 9. And you'll see that in practice in the next section in this course.

Now basic modules don't officially exist in JDK 9 either. We just use the term basic for a module that is not an open module. Now in other words these are modules that are not automatic and not open. So it's got the same characteristics as a normal module except that it's not an open module. So let's talk about open modules now many third-party libraries like spring and hibernate use reflection to access the internals of JDK of the JDK at runtime.

Now these libraries won't work unless we have an open module. Now an open module is defined using the open keyword. Now an open module makes all packages inside the module accessible for deep reflection. Now the keyword open can be used to declare an open module or to declare specific packages as open. Now you will get to see this in action later in the course with a java fx application. We're going to see how to open some packages for the fxml loader and the application class.

All right. So unnamed modules which we talked about earlier in this video. Well, they don't have a name and also, we don't declare them. Now they export all their packages, and it actually reads all modules in the JDK and on the module path. Now an unnamed module is a module made up of jar files from the class path, and all these jar files form the unnamed module. And what we will do later is discuss the difference between the module path and class path.

And importantly a named module can't require an unnamed module. All right. So let's talk now about aggregator modules. Now these exist for convenience. Now usually they have no code of their own, they just have a module descriptor. And they collect and export the contents of other modules. This is the reason why they're named as an aggregator. Now it's an example here when a few modules depend on, let's say, three modules. What we can do is create an aggregator module for those three modules.

And that way our modules can depend on only a single module which would be that newly created aggregator model. And if you want to see an example of that in the JDK 9, there's several aggregator modules. Take a look in java.se that module for starters. All right. So module path and class path JDK 9 introduced a module path. Now a module path can represent a path to a sequence of folders that contain modules. It can represent a path to a modular java file, it can represent a path to a jmod file which if you're unfamiliar is an extended version of a jar file.

And we will discuss jmod files later in the course. Now a module path is used by the compiler here to find and resolve modules. Every module from a module path needs to have a module declaration and again is the module-info.java file. So contrasting that the module path to a class path, the class path, of course, just represents a sequence of java files. All right. So let's finish this video here, and we'll continue our discussion in the next video.

LECTURE 27.7: Understanding and Implementing Transitive Dependencies for Simplified Module
----------------------------------------

All right. So let's find out about transitive dependencies and the module graph. Then we're going to update our project to use these transitive dependencies. So what is a transitive dependency? Well, let's say we've got three modules, a, b and c. Now when module a requires module b. Then module a can read public and protected types exported in module b. Now if module b also requires module c, then module b can have methods that return types exported in module c.

So let's see within our project. So in our project, we've got three modules common DB and UI. Now the module DB requires and reads common, while module UI reads both DB and common. Now module DB or actually the data source class has some methods that return types from module common. So every module that uses the data source class will require common module as well. Now this is where transitive dependencies can help us. So instead of adding a require statement to the UI module, we can use the keyword transitive with the require statement.

So that way every module that reads the DB module will then automatically be able to read the common module. So let's see an image just to clarify this further. So this image we've got the module graph. Now the result of java modules depending on each other is that we can now draw a complete graph of dependencies with the modules as nodes and the relationship between nodes as module dependencies. Now this kind of image is called a module graph. Now keep in mind that this graph only shows our modules not other modules that we're using like javafx.base, for example.

So what does this have to do with transitive dependencies? Well, you can see how our UI module depends on both the common and DB modules. Remember that the data source class returns some types from the common module and the UI module is using the data source class to get results from the database. So instead of requiring the common module in the UI module, we can declare it as a transitive dependency in the DB module. So that way whatever modules use the DB module, again, we'll also have access to the UI module.

So let's clarify this further with another image. So this image is now showing the transitive dependency. So as you can now see the module DB requires the module common by using the transitive keyword. So that way all modules that require the DB module now have access to packages that are exported by the common module. And we don't then have to specify the requires common module in the UI module because it now reads it automatically. So let's hop back now into intellij and see if we can set this up.

So firstly, we need to open our module info java file from the DB module. I've got that open up here, click it if relevant to the relevant module info file, but we're in our DB one here. So what we need to do is make a change here and use the transitive keyword for the common dependency. So we come up here to line four, and I'm going to type requires where it's just got academy.learnprogramming.com. It's going to be transitive space and then the module name academy.learnprogramming.com.

So now the UI module can have access to all exported packages by the common module. So in other words, we don't need to depend on the common module anymore in the UI module. Let's go ahead and open the UI module descriptor file. Again, just check you're in the right file there. And what we want to do here is we no longer need to the requires for our common module. This is what the transitive keyword is going to do for us. So now that we've done that bearing in mind that we are requiring the DB module. And of course,we just made the change to the DB module.

So now that we've done that, we should see that we can still be able -- we are still able to run our application. So as you can see that's working nicely everything's working so it should do there. So again, with transitive dependencies we then don't have to require, we don't need to require every single module. So what other required statements can be removed. Well, let's just have a look at the one we've got on screen now the UI module descriptor file.

You can see that we've got five required statements. Four of them are java fx related. Then we've got the DB module. Now we can hold down the control or command key and click on a module name, for example, javafx.base. And let's just take a look at that so we can see here what packages are exported by default. In the last few videos we saw how to create our first programme in Java. It was pretty basic to say the least printing out some text on the screen but it was a good place to start. But if we wanted to start getting the computer to do something useful, we need to start using variables. So what are variables? Well, variables are a way to store information in our computer. Variables that we define in a programme can be accessed by a name we give them, and the computer does the hard work of figuring out where they get stored in the computers Random Access Memory or RAM.

Now a variable as the name suggests can be changed, in other words its contents are variable. So what we have to do is tell the computer what type of information we wanna store in the variable and then give the variable a name. There are lots of different types of data that we can define for our variables. Collectively these are known as data types. As you may have guessed data types are key words in Java. So let's start out by defining a variable of type int, int being an abbreviation for integer which was a whole number, that is a number without any decimal points.

To define a variable we need to specify the data type then give our variable a name and optionally add an expression to initialize the variable with a value. And we'll talk more about expression shortly. And finally we added that semicolon to end the line and a form a statement. So the semicolon ends the line and tells Java, just that that the lines complete.

So this entire line as we've typed is a statement or to be more specific it's a declaration statement. So a declaration statement is used to define a variable by indicating the data type, and the name, then optionally to set the variable to a certain value. So here the type, and type is a shortcut for the word data type is an int, the name is my first number and the value were assigning or initialising our variable with is five. So we're declaring a variable of type int with the name my first number and assigning the value of five to it.

So if you don't specify a type that you actually wanna convert to, then the integer is assumed automatically by Java, and you saw that in these cases, we got an error because of that. LECTURE 31.17: Method Overloading Recap
----------------------------------------

So let's have a bit of a recap on what we've learnt about method overloading and discuss the benefits of by using method overloading. So confirming again as a recap that method overloading is a feature that allows us to have more than one method with the same name so long as we use different arguments or parameters so it's the ability to create multiple methods of the same name with different implementations, calls to an overloaded method will run a specific implementation or version if you will of that method. Now in the example from the previous video, we had the calculate score method that had 0 1 & 2 parameters.

As an example let's say that you have to create a method which can do the sum of two numbers the sum of three numbers and the sum of four numbers. Now each method would have parameters passed to it with the numbers to sum, so ending up with the following methods in this example is not good practice and actually is not method overloading so you'd never want to write code like I'm showing you below because it's considered bad practice and you can see in a scenario we've got three methods of different names to remember.

So the main problem here with these methods is that you have to remember three method names that do the sum. Now imagine that you wanted to have a method that adds up to 20 numbers. you've effectively end up having to write 20 different methods with 20 different names, remembering 20 names would be quite hard so to overcome this problem we can use the same name for the method, let's see an example of that so a solution to that problem with method overloading would still end up with three methods but note that they're now all sharing the same method name much easy to remember so we've got a method that sums overloaded twice with two three or four parameters so that's an example of how the method should be written in other words we can use the method overloading feature and write methods with the same name so that way we just need to remember one name of the method which in this case is sum. Alright so let's now see both examples at once so at the top there we've got the bad practice and that's with the three different method names and again the reason we're not doing that is firstly it's not method overloading but secondly it's hard to remember method names that are different there in the

example below, we've got three methods with the same name we just have to remember one method name and it gives us more flexiblity, you can see how method overloading can be very helpful when scenarios like this you keep in mind that method overloading is a very common thing it's used everywhere and in many other languages as well. So as an example the println method which of course is part of Java that's a great example of method overloading there's actually ten methods with the same name println in Java and that's allowing us to print an integer print a double print a string and so on. So you can see that's a good example of method overloading, so as a final recap on method overloading, it improves code readability and reusability, it's easier to remember one method name instead of remembering multiple names, it achieves consistency in naming so one name four methods that are commonly used and as an example println from the java language itself and finally overloaded methods give programmers the flexibility to call a similar method with different types of data based on the arguments or parameters that you define so that's the method overloading recap, let's now move on to the next video.

Alright, so let's recap what we've learnt so far about arrays and discuss some of the common errors that occur with arrays. So for example 10 elements the index range would be from 0 through 9. Now if we try to access an index that is out of range Java will give us an array index out of bounds exception that which indicates that the index is out of range in other words, out of bounds we're trying to access an element that is outside of what we've defined. To access array elements, we use square braces this is also known as the array access operator.

So let's see an example of how to create an array, so we use square brackets after the type in this case it's an int array so we've got int square braces then the name of variable in this case array so it's int square brackets array then after the equal sign we type new int in this case since it's an int array and 5 and square braces representing the number of elements in the array, in other words the length of the array. So you can see in this scenario that the array contains the elements from array 0 through to array 4, it's got 5 elements and the index range in this example is 0 to 4 the new operator or keyword is used to create the array and initialize the array elements to their default values, remembering that an int in this case will be defaulted to 0. Now for boolean type arrays if we use boolean instead of int they would all be initialized to false, if you use string or other objects they would be set to null but we'll be talking more about null and what that is later in the course. So this example here we've got int left and right square braces my numbers equals and we've got left to right curly braces with the numbers 5 4 3 2 1 in it then at the end theirs's a semicolon. So this is a way to

initialize an array inline using an array initializer block and that's what that is there the left and right curly braces with contents in between and notice that we're defining the values for the array separated by a comma. So this way of initializing is also known as an anonymous array it's got five elements and the index range is 0 through 4 and in this example you've probably figured out that the array elements are initialized to 5 4 3 2 1. Alright, here's another example of our array int square braces my array equals new int 5 and in square braces and a semicolon you may recall that when we first used variables, a set of variable is a place in memory, so think of it like a box that you could store something and you can store something in that box, well the same goes for arrays but with arrays you can imagine an array it's a row of boxes of slots where each box can contain a value, so in other words we could store something into each box so in this example I mentioned we created an array with five elements so in other words five boxes and they are by default all initialized to zero, so every box in this example contains an integer value of zero, so every box or slots got an index so that we can access the values

by an index using square braces, so in this example we've initialized the array with values in the same line using an array initializer as we talked about and that's also known as I mentioned as an anonymous array. Now each box or slot contains a value the array again has five elements, but we're putting the values into each box so each box has got a different value so the box or element index 0 contains number 10 the box at array element 1 contains 35 and so on. Alright, so our second common error happens when you loop through an array, now there's a logic error in other words we're starting here from element one but remember that the array index starts from zero, so if we printed out the elements of the array starting from index 1 the first element which is at index zero won't be printed in this scenario, so if this ever happens to you just change the variable in the for loop to start at zero, so you can see

LECTURE 33.14: Autoboxing and Unboxing
----------------------------------------

So in this video we're going to talk about the concept of auto boxing and unboxing. So to start with we're just gonna have a little brief recap of arrays and array lists and we'll move on to autoboxing. So firstly, you're aware that we can do something like this, no doubt because we've actually been through this in the code creating a regular array. Let's just call that stringArray equals new String(10). And likewise we could do that for an integer if we wanted to new int(10) so that's creating array.

You've seen that before, Of ten elements starting from position, element 0 through 9 and we can also create an array list. We can do ArrayList String. You've seen this before and we'll call that string arrayList = new arrayList like so. And we can use that and then we can do something like stringArrayList.add "Tim". And that would add an element to the arrayList and we would actually add an object of the type string to the arrayList for us automatically.

But interestingly enough, what we can't do is something like this. We can't do an arrayList int int arrayList = new ArrayList. We actually get an error. And the error we actually get is, type argument cannot be of primitive type. And this, as it turns out, is an issue because a primitive type is not a class. And we actually need, a class reference here, to be able to use that to be able to save something to an arrayList. So, if we had a list of integers, we can't save them based on what we know so far of Java, in an arrayList.

What we could do, for example, we could do something like this, we could create a class. I'm just going to create it in here, we can put create, and we'll do type in class, and we'll call it intClass. We can have a private int myValue. We can add a constructor. So in this video, we're gonna start talking about a linked list. This is another type of list and we've already dealt with arrays in general. We've talked about those extensively and of course we also talked about the ArrayList and we've used that quite a bit in the code as well. So the linked list is another type of list. So just as a recap, you will need to know this because of the way that linked lists work. We've already seen that an array's an index list of items.

So they can be primitive types for example, ints, doubles, booleans those types of things in the case of a normal array. Or of course we can also use objects in the case of an ArrayList and actually store them like that. So we've seen how to access individual elements by using an index. So the sixth item, for example, would be found at index position five. So just as a quick recap, let's just look at this on the screen. You can see there that we've actually got an array on screen of seven integers.

So in the index position to the left is the number that we use to access the particular value. So the first element of course we use index position 0. Grabs the value 34, index position 1, grabs the value of 18, so on and so forth. Now what happens internally, and this is important to get a good understanding of linked lists, is that java will actually allocate four bytes of memory, for each integer. Because it needs up to that amount to be able to store the highest value integer, and we have talked about that in much earlier in the course, about how that memory works.

So, you can see what happens there is that Java will try to do this continuously. So you can see in this case what its done, theirs actually a formula that Java can used to actually figure out which address, which physical memory address to use to grab the value. So what it can do quite simply, it can look at the base address. This is actually for the first element in the array. So this would be index position 0. So you can actually use that formula, and what it can actually do is calculate the actual address based on that.

So in other words, looking at the base address, which in this case is 100 plus four times the index number. So for example, if we want to get access to the actual third index position. Se we would actually do we would multiply index position 3 by 4 because four bytes in each integer so that's 3 times 4 is 12. We would add that to our base address which was 100 which was the first element. And that would give us an answer of 112 and you can see on the screen there that index position 3, it's value is 112.

So that's how Java sort of handles things internally and this type of thing works for primitive types much the same way. In the example of a double for arguments sake well it uses up to eight bytes of memory for each double, because it needs that for floating point numbers. So the same formula would apply, we would actually still do the calculation but instead of doing, multiplying by four, for four bytes for an integer. We multiply by eight, which is eight bytes for a double.

So that works fine for primitive types where you've got a known value and it's always gonna be the same length. For example, an integer is always going to consume four bytes of memory. A double will always consume eight bytes. But what about strings? Strings don't actually work the same, do they? Because strings of course can be a variable size. And this also applies in general to objects as well. So as you can see on the screen, now I'm gonna switch to the next slide.

What's actually happening here is that we've got the same index to the left-hand side, the same array. This time it's actually got strings instead of integers, and we've got the same number. And you can see that there's actually a calculation there. It's eight bytes. So what's happening is that the memory that's being allocated in the array is actually itself eight bytes. But that actually points to another location in memory where the string is.

So consequently by doing that, Java can actually keep a track of the actual strings that are in the array and also the strings can each be a variable length, so they can be different lengths. Because of course strings can be a variable length to unlike an integer which has to be and always is four bytes. So, you can see the important concept there. Array, index position 0, which is at a memory location, 100. It's got a string address of 1034 and then, looking at the memory address of a position on the address of 1034, it's actually got the string value.

In this case, of Tim. And likewise, we looked at another one for argument's sake. Index position 3. Well, that's got a string address of 1024 and that points to the Hello World as a string. So, that's what's happening internally. Now if we actually printed that out we actually went through and did a for loop and actually printed that out. The actual order that would come out is actually Tim, Australia, Java, Hello World, Done, Array and ArrayList.

Because of course it's actually going through the index positions from 0 to 6. So its looking at the first one pointing to a 1024, Tim. Looking at the next one, index position one, 1037, Australia. Looking at position two, 1046 is the string address, that's gonna be Java. So on and so forth. So requesting the stringed index position three causes java to calculate the address of that item in the array. So 100 + 3 x 8 bytes = 124. That's this location here.

But it then actually uses the string address to actually find the actual string. So that's what's actually happening internally by Java automatically. It's not something you need to know too much about. Another thing to note is, with all these strings over here to the right hand side once your program stops executing, or goes out of scope in some way, and then the variables are no longer needed and there's this process called Java's Garbage collection which goes through automatically and frees up that memory.

So it releases it. So it can actually be used again. So that again has all been happening behind the scenes, and it's not something you need to worry about. And just a final point here to make is that the actual string addresses do not need to be contiguous. So in other words you can see here that one of the string address here for index position 4 is actually address 4000, but some of the other ones have got completely different numbers. So the point here is that things can be completely different, and that's the way that it happens and it's done internally by Java.

LECTURE 34.1: Interfaces
----------------------------------------

In this video we're gonna start talking about interfaces. So an interface, in Java terms, specifies methods that a particular class that implements the interface must implement. Now the interface itself that you're creating is abstract, and that means that there's no actual code for any of the methods, you only supply the actual method names and the parameters. The actual code still goes in the actual class that you're creating. But the idea is to use an interface to provide a common behavior that can be used by several classes by having them all implement the same interface.

So it's really a way to standardize the way a particular set of classes is used. So looking at an example, if we have a look at a simple class that I've created, called GearBox, you can see that there's a private boolean field there called clutchIsIn. And there's a simple public method there called operateClutch, which is sent a parameter called in or out and if the string value is set to the value in then clutch is in boolean field is actually set to true otherwise it's set to false.

So that's just one way of implementing a particular method to decide whether the clutch is in, in a GearBox class, but that's probably not the best way of doing it. It's a little bit untidy. So if we wanted to actually do something different, we might decide that we wanted to actually change this here to boolean. Like so, boolean in or out and then we can do something like this clutches in equals in or out. And that's certainly valid code and it does work, but the problem would be then that the actual signature, in other words this component of the public method, has been changed.

And if you've got some other code that is reliant on the fact that this first parameter was a string, as it originally was, and we've changed it to a boolean code. It means we've broken that other code in the sense that, that then has to be changed. That code has to be changed as well. And if you're using a very popular framework or your code is used in a lot of other places, this could be a serious problem and it's not something that becomes immediately aware if other programs are actually using your GearBox classes, class in example.

The problem actually is that although we've created this GearBox class, we haven't really made a sort of you know a commitment if you will that won't be changed. In other words we haven't said that once we create this particular public method, we aren't going to change it. So what the interface is is just that. It's actually a commitment, a contract if you will, that the method's signatures and that those variables in the interface constants if you defined any will not change.

So consequently, you can create an interface and use it and you'll know that provided you stick to what's in that interface, the code isn't going to change and you're not gonna be breaking code anywhere. So let's actually go ahead and create an interface and talk more about how it actually works. We're now going to create an interface to define the behavior of a telephone. So I'm gonna come up here to my package as normal click on new. I'm actually going to select class, but then I'm going to come down here and select interface.

So I'm going to actually type the interface name and by convention you normally type I as the first letter, capital I for the fact that it's interface. So we're going to say I telephone, which means it's an interface named telephone. And you notice there's a slight variation, GearBox the class has got public class GearBox, but in interface uses the word interface instead of class. Then what we actually do is we want to define just the methods, in this case that we're going to be or that are gonna be used in this interface that a class that implements this interface needs to actually implement.

So let's move ahead and actually do that. So I'm gonna type public void power on, that would be a function of a telephone to power it on. Public Void Dial. We're going to dial, we're going to set the parameter, phone number and notice how I'm not actually creating classes. I'm creating what's called the signature. So this is the parameters, the name, the return type and any parameters, but we're not actually defining the actual actual code itself.

That still goes into the class that inherits this interface. So we're just defining the actual methods that form this interface. So answer would be another one. We'll try another one. Public boolean call phone. We want to return a status to see whether we're successful or not. Boolean phone number would be the parameter. Let's do another one just to determine whether the phone is ringing, IsRinging. So that's a simple interface. So again, all we've done here, we've said, for a class that is going to implement them from this interface, these are the methods that it has to implement.

So you don't write code in the interface as such. You still write that in the class, which you're about to see, but we've just defined here the contract. In other words, the contract and the actual parameters and return types that are valid for each method, that overall will make this a valid class, effectively. And notice also that public actually appears, and it actually says it's redundant for interface methods. And that actually makes sense if you think about it.

And that's because we're actually implementing the interface in a class, so the interface exists to define the methods that must be implemented. So in other words, private or public is really useless, in essence, because you're gonna be doing that in the actual class. So you could actually, if you wanted to, remove this altogether because we don't actually need, whoops, we don't actually need that access modifier. So that's quite valid to do that as well.

So now that we've actually done that, how would we go about implementing this interface? In other words, how do we go about defining a class and saying our class is going to be using this interface? Well to do that we're going to create a new class first. I'm going to create a new class called desk phone and this will be a regular class, so just call it desk phone. And the way you actually get it to use the interface is, you use the implements keyword.

So you type implements, now type in I and it should automatically find the interface. You can see the I telephone interface is found for us. So we've done that now. As soon as we've actually typed that in, we're getting a red error. And the error actually is class deskphone must either be declared abstract or implement the abstract method powerOn, and it's actually the those other methods as well. So what it's actually saying is we need to start implementing some of these things in order for this to become a valid class.

So there's a couple of ways forward, you can actually do this automatically you can create the basic methods. You can create stubs for these methods, which means you can create empty methods and implement these if you want or you can type them manually. So I'm going to actually type a few. So I'm going to type MyNumber for starters which will be the phone number and let's do another one private boolean IsRinging. IsRinging. So to go ahead and actually create them, you're going to actually go up and do, notice here implement methods we haven't actually used that before but if we actually click on that, it automatically went into the interface for i telephone, and its found all these methods that says do you want to implement these.

I'm gonna click on, yes I'm just gonna leave the option to select for all of them, click on okay, and you notice it's now overrode each one of those functions, and suddenly the class is now quite happy because we've actually done them all. Just to confirm, if we delete say the second one, we'll get an error again because not all the methods have been implemented. So again, what we're trying to do here is we're trying to say that in order to be a valid class, we're saying that for a telephone class that is in our application, these are the five methods that must be implemented with the appropriate parameters.

And where appropriate, with the appropriate return types being void or an actual Type. And at that point we can then go away and actually create some code if we wanted to. We could do something simple, for example with a desktop phone there's probably no one button that's probably always on, so we could type something in there. No action taken. Desk phone does not have a power button. For the dial now ringing. So recording the functionality for this particular type of phone.

For answer, we want to check first to see whether it was ringing, so we put if is ringing. Answering the desk phone. And we will set is ringing to false because we answered it. Pretty simple. And say for call phone if phone number is equal to my number. IsRinging equals true. else IsRinging equals false. And we'll return isRinging. Just a very simple concocted example here just to show the concept of the interface. And lastly, isRinging, we're gonna actually return the variable isRinging to see whether that's true or false.

So although the interface relies on all these methods even if you don't want to use it. So for example, with the desktop phone, you might have decided that we're not going to have a power on button, we still need to implement it. The implementation can be simple, in other words overriding that function that's actually just putting an error message to say not supported or not needed for this type of telephone if that makes sense. So the way to decide that generally, is to really consider the relationship of the final class to the object that it's extending or implementing.

So in other words, with our telephone example both devices have a telephone so the desk phone doesn't have anything else. I mean, really can do far more than make or receive phone calls, so it's more accurate to say that a mobile phone is actually a computer that has a phone interface.

So you can say that a desk phone can telephone and a mobile phone can telephone, which indicates that they should both implement a phone interface rather than extending a phone class if that makes sense. So they both inherit from the animal class. But a dog can walk so it implements walk.

So it's now time to talk about inner classes because the thing is in Java, it's actually possible to nest a class inside another class. So what I'm gonna do is start by outlining the four types of nested classes, and then we'll go through some examples. So the four types of nested classes that you can use in Java are static nested classes. We could use a nonstatic nested class and we call that an inner class. We use a local class, now that's an inner class that's defined inside of a scope block which is usually a method and also an anonymous class which is a nested class without a class name.

Now, the static nested class is mainly used to associate a class with its outer class. So in terms of behavior, you'd think of it as being identical to a top level class, but the difference is that it's packaged in its outer class rather than in the package. So that really means that it cannot access the nonstatic methods or members of its outer class without first creating an instance of that class. So I know that sounds like a mouthful. So in this set of videos we're gonna start talking about Abstractions. So abstraction is when you define the required functionality for something without actually implementing the details. In other words we're focusing on what needs to be done, not on the how it's to be done. So, interface is, as you saw, are purely abstract, and they don't specify any actual aspect of the implementation. The actual implementation, of course, was left to the classes that implement the interface, and that's why we use the word implements when we're using an interface.

And as you can see, I've got the challenge from the interfaces set of videos. And I'm just gonna go through and just confirm that again. So you can see that we've got our interface here. In this case say Monster, and that's actually implements that's implementing the Isavable interface meaning that it's actually gonna do the work. So the ISaveable interface, as you can see onscreen, provided, or specified that there must be a write method that returned an ArrayList of values to be saved, and also the read method.

As you can see on the screen, there that was provided with an ArrayList of values to be restored. So there weren't any other details of how the class should populate, or write the ArrayList. No details on what the class should do with the read values either, that's left entirely up to each individual class.
