LECTURE 34.10: Interface vs Abstract Class
----------------------------------------

All right. So let's discuss the main differences between an abstract class and an interface and when to use either of them. And this should hopefully give you a better overall understanding of both. So firstly, an abstract class. Well, these are very similar to interfaces. You cannot instantiate them, and they may contain a mix of methods declared with or without an implementation. However, with abstract classes, you can declare fields that are not static and final and define public, protected and private concrete methods.

An abstract class can extend only one parent class. However, it can implement multiple interfaces. Now when an abstract class is subclassed, the subclass usually provides implementations for all of the abstract methods in its parent class. However, if it doesn't, then the subclass must also be declared abstract. So you want to use an abstract class when, firstly, you want to share code among several closely related classes, animal, for example, with field's name, age and so on.

Or if you expect classes that extend your abstract class to have many common methods or fields or required access modifiers other than public so protected in private. You may also want to use an abstract class where you want to declare non-static or non-final fields. For example, name and age. So this then enables you to define methods that can access and modify the state of an object, getname, setname and so forth. And also, you may want to use an abstract class when you've got a requirement for your base class to provide a default implementation of certain methods, but other methods should be open to being overwritten by child classes.

As a general summary, the purpose of an abstract class is to provide a common definition of a base class that multiple derived classes can share. All right. Interfaces. So an interface is just the declaration of methods of a class, it's not the implementation. Now in an interface, we define what kind of operation an object can perform. Now these operations are defined by the classes that implement the interface. So interfaces form a contract between the class and the outside world and this contract is enforced at build time by the java compiler.

Now you cannot instantiate interfaces and they may contain a mix of methods declared with or without an implementation. Now all methods and interfaces are automatically public and abstract. Now an interface can extend another interface. Interfaces are more flexible and can deal with a lot more stress on the design of your program than the implementation. Now by introducing interfaces into your program, you're really introducing points of variation at which you can plug in different implementations for that interface.

Now a interface's primary purpose is abstraction decoupling the what from the how. And just a couple of general notes here, since java 8 interfaces can now contain default methods, so in other words methods with implementation. Now the keyword default is used mostly for backwards compatibility and static methods as well before java 8, that wasn't possible. And since java 9 and interface can also contain private methods commonly used when 2 default methods in an interface share common code.

All right. So when do you want to use an interface. Well, firstly, when you expect that unrelated classes will implement your interface. For example, the interfaces comparable and cloneable are implemented by many unrelated classes. Now another reason to use an interface is when you want to specify the behavior of a particular data type, but you're not concerned about who implements its behavior. Still another reason for using an interface if you want to separate different behavior.

Now the collections API in java is an excellent example of interfaces. We've got the list interface and implementations array list and linked list among others and more on this later in the course. Another example is the JDBC API. Now that exists of almost only interfaces. The concrete implementation of methods are provided as JDBC drivers. So that enables you to write all the JDBC code independent of the database the db vendor, and you'll learn more about JDBC in this course.

So that's the differences between abstract classes and interfaces. Let's move on now to the next video.

So if a bug appears in production code, production here means the code that has been released to the Google store or it's commercially available or it's not test code anymore, it has to be fixed.

There's no doubts about it that for most bugs, so some minor bugs that perhaps you wouldn't need to fix, but ultimately if it's in production mode there must be fixed and so what is fixing it the code itself must be then fully tested to insure that the actual fixing made didn't in fact introduce another bug. And then of course finally the updated code containing the fix or fixes has to actually be redeployed and uploaded to the Google store or it what it whichever Android app store you're actually using.

So, lambda expressions, often called lambdas, are a new feature introduced with Java 8. And what they do is they provide us with an easier way to work with interfaces that have only got one method. And typically, they are often used in places where we use anonymous classes, and you'll see what I mean as we progress through the videos in this section of the course.

But let's start by reviewing how we use a runnable object to create and run a thread, and then we'll see how this relates to lambdas. And the code would be new Thread new. Code to run closing parentheses .start. So, it's not something you haven't seen a number of times before. So, we run this. Okay, printing for the mobiles. Printing from the rotable and here we just put our parentheses right through parentheses .start, and we can obviously kick it off that way using an anonymous class. and obviously give us the same result. And we get the same result so that's a lambda expression. Now, every lambda expression has got three parts; first one is the argument list, the second one is an arrow token, and thirdly the body. So, let's take a closer look at what we wrote here. The lambda expression we used, and specifically what we're talking about is this code here, that I've got highlighted. So, this expression has an empty argument list. The arrow token is just the dash character followed by the greater than character.

So, we can refer to that as the arrow token. Now, the body is the code that we want to run which in this case is the system.out.println statement. Now, when the compiler sees a lambda expression, how does it know what to do? Well, it knows that one of the thread classes constructors accepts a runnable parameter, and in addition it also knows that the runnable interface only has one method, in this case “run”, which doesn't take any parameters. So, it's able to match the lambda expressions argument list with no parameters with the run method.

Now, because the compiler needs to match the lambda expression to a method, lambda expressions can only be used with interfaces that contain only one method that has to be implemented. So, these interfaces are also referred to as functional interfaces. Now, by using a lambda expression, instead of creating a class that implements runnable, or using an anonymous class, we're actually able to reduce the lines of code we have to write. And we could focus on what we care about, in this case the code we want to run.

Now, before we move on, notice that intellij recognizes lambdas and marks them with the lambda symbol. So, that's a really handy way to quickly check that the expression matches the method that I would have to implement, if we weren't using a lambda.

Now, throughout this section, I've intentionally written Lambda expressions in different ways. Here are the variations that I've used. First one was specify the types of parameters versus letting the compiler infer them. The second one was using a return statement with curly braces, for one statement Lambda expressions, versus not using return because it's implied, and hence not requiring curly braces, three, using lambda expressions that contain one statement, versus Lambda expressions that have more than one statement.

And for using parentheses with a lambda expression only has one argument versus not using parentheses, since they're optional when there's only one argument. So, if you look at the four variations, the two alternatives offer the choice between verbosity or verbosity, I should say, versus conciseness, which in turn often comes down to the choice between readability and conciseness. Not all the time. Of course, short, Lambda expressions are usually readable, no matter how concise they are.

But when striving for conciseness, we can sometimes write lambda expressions that are difficult to decipher, because we've left out too much information. Now, there are a number of articles and tutorials on the internet that discuss best practices when using lambda expressions. Now, many of them fall on the side of conciseness. But keep in mind that best practices are guidelines Not rules. So, when writing code that I haven't written or going back to code that I wrote months or years ago, previously, it's actually not unusual for me to come across a lambda expression that's cryptic, and takes a lot of work to figure out.

So, the question I would ask is, was it concise? Well, yes, it was. But was it readable to the human? No. So, yes, we can optionally leave out the parameter types when the compiler can infer them. But will it be easier for a developer reading the code to do the same? Yeah, we don't have to include the return keyword when a one statement lambda returns a value. But will a developer be able to tell at a glance what the layer or that the lambda expression returns a value.

So, in my opinion, when it comes down to practices that are syntactic and don't make a difference to the code that's generated, the key thing here is to be consistent. So, don't use different styles within the same file. If you're working on code someone else wrote, and they always leave out the parameter types, then you should do the same. If they always use the return keyword with one statement, lambdas do the same. If you're writing code from scratch, do what's clearer and the easiest for you, but also what you think will be clearer for other developers who may work on the code in the future.

Personally, I'd rather see a verbose lambda than a concise form with a comment because I know from experience that comments are always updated when the code is and that can ultimately lead to a lot of confusion and wasted time. So when you're actually importing classes from another package, you can actually choose to import the entire package. And notice that IntelliJ did that on line 3 with the Java.awt.star. Or of course, as you saw in lines four and five, you can actually just specify the class of interfaces that you actually need.

So there's really no right or wrong way about this. There's lots of heated debate about the pros and cons. One thing, though, you should be aware of, if you are actually using something like line three, where you're putting a star. There's a possible impact if you've got a new class of interfaces added to one of the packages you actually import. So if the other package contains a class or an interface with the same name, then your program's not going to compile.

So you might think that's unlikely to happen, but it does actually happen. One example was with the java.awt package. So there's actually several reasons I actually chose to use this package for the example here and this is one of them. So in Java 1.1, which I know was a very long time ago, the java.awt.package contained a list class. This was often imported as java.awt.star and of course Java.util.package is also imported as java.util.star, and everything worked fine then.

But in Java 1.2, sun included a list interface in java.util and of course we've used the list interface quite a bit. So the programs importing these two packages continue to run. But because Java actually compiles the fully qualified class names In the compiled code. But the point here, and this is the big point, when one of the programs needed to be changed, it wouldn't compile anymore. And that's because the entire package has been imported, the star in other words.

So Java actually had no idea which of the two packages the list was actually referring to. Was at the list class in java.awt or the new list interface in java.util? So, if it was a different programmer, making changes to the program, they'll probably be cursing the original programmer for leaving code in there that didn't even compile, when in fact the code had been fine when it had been left. So the problem arose because of a change in a third party library.

So explicitly importing the class, the list class, in other words, not using the star, would have actually avoided that problem altogether. So the thing is with Scope it's probably one of the easiest things about programming, once you understand it, but it's actually also one of the most confusing Until you do actually understand it. So scope here actually refers to the visibility of a class, member, or variable.

So to consider that in non-computing terms, let's imagine you're going to buy a particular computer, and you find a local store and let's just say it's got the computer for 20% off, 20% discount. Now, the same computer in another store would still be at the full price, though. So the scope, in other words, or the price reduction is just that one local store. But, contrast that to a situation where you've got a large company, and let's use Wal Mart as an example.

Huge company in the United States, and say if they decided to discount a particular computer, so the discount then would actually apply in about 4,500 stores across America. So in that context the scope of the discount is therefore much much wider. And that actually as walmart is a multi national company. If they applied the discount world wide, the scope would be over 11,000 stores. So the important thing here is that Walmart's discount does not apply to any other stores.

So the scope is limited to the stores controlled only by Walmart. And the same with the local example, the local store that had the 20% off. The scope there is just for that one local store. So the same computer and in a Java context would be the same variable. In other stores, it's not discounted. I hope that makes sense. Our Java objects have got scope in much the same way. LECTURE 39.1: Collections Overview

So back in section 9, we looked at 3 of java's list types that was the list interface, the array list and also the linked list classes. Now those form part of the java collections framework and that framework also includes things like sets, maps, trees and queues. So at the top level of the collections framework is the collections class. Now this exposes static methods that either operate on collections such as the sort method that we've used previously or they also return collections objects such as the list method.

Now the interfaces in the collection framework what they do is they allow the framework to be extended. And they actually define methods for all the fundamental operations that really are required for the various collection types. Now one of the design goals of the collections framework was that there should be good interoperability amongst various collections. So not just the one's included in the framework. But literally anything that may also be created in the future that is a reasonable representation of a collection.

Now that also includes arrays. Now arrays themselves couldn't be made part of the collection framework without changing the java language. However, the framework does include methods that enable collections to be moved into arrays and vice versa and additionally methods to allow rays to be viewed as collections. So the main components or the core elements of the collections framework are interfaces. Now these are the abstract types that represent collections, including the list interface that we've already seen, as mentioned previously.

And we will be looking at the interface hierarchy of the collections framework. Also included is aggregate operations. Now although we've seen iterators in earlier videos, we'll cover them in much more detail here in this section. In addition, another core element is implementations. This is the concrete implementations of the interface, including the array list and linked list classes that's 2 good examples of an implementation. But also algorithms.

Now the java JDK provides a range of polymorphic algorithms that work on collections objects, technically speaking on objects that implement the collection interface, and they provide reusable functionality. So I'll be looking at all these elements in this section. Although I'll do so by working with the framework rather than producing a video on each element. We could even use a map type as the values in another map. In actual fact, you could add a map as a value to itself although it's probably not a good idea to do that. It's important to point out that unlike other languages, such as python, for example, there's no requirement that the keys of a map be immutable.

And just as a recap immutable objects are things like strings and integers whose value can't change. If that sounds strange when we assign a new string value to a string variable, a variable what we're doing is we're changing the value that the variable holds. We're not changing the string so algol for example that we used for 1 of the keys earlier that's on line 21 can't be changed. On the other hand, an array list can change by having new items added or new values assigned to existing entries.

Now with that said, the java documentation does warn that great care must be exercised if immutable objects are used as map keys. So they give you that warning but they're not prohibited. Now the reason for the warning is that a map object can behave unpredictably if the key objects change in such a way that equals comparisons are affected. Remember, we talked about those equal comparisons in the last video and actually earlier in this video. So it's worth being aware of this warning, but you'll probably have to do something fairly advanced before it affects. You so using classes as keys is in itself fairly advanced.

Now one thing that's not permitted is for a map to contain itself as a key. And it would be a very bizarre program that attempted to do such a thing. LECTURE 39.11: Sets & HashSet
----------------------------------------

So let's have a talk about the set interface as well as hashset. So sets are generally used less often than lists and maps, but they can in themselves be extremely useful. Now where a list is an ordered collection of items that can contain duplicates, a set has no defined ordering, number one, and the oracle documentation defines it as chaotic. But secondly, a set cannot contain duplicates so very important distinctions there. In actual fact, the lack of duplicates is the most important differentiator as there are ordered sets, such as the linked hashset and treeset that we'll look at together with the corresponding map objects in a later video.

Now if you want to ensure that that there's no duplicates in your collection, then a good way of doing that is to use a set rather than a list. Now the set interface, just like everything else in the collections framework, is generic and it takes a single type. Just like maps and lists, it's possible to create a raw set, but this is intended really for backwards compatibility with code created before generics were added to the java language. And generally speaking, it's not a good idea to do that.

Now the set interface defines the basic methods add, remove and clear to maintain the items in the set as well as offering a size method and isempty to provide some information about how much or how many items are actually in the set and whether it's empty or not. Now we can also check if an item, a specific item is in the set using the contains method. Now interestingly enough there's no way to retrieve an item from a set. You can check if something exists and you can iterate over all the elements in the set, but attempting to get say for example the tenth element from a set isn't possible.

You need to use a list to do something like that. Now we've already used a set when looking at maps. The keys in a map can be retrieved as a set using the key set method, which we talked about before. So it's therefore not surprising that everything we said about keys in a map also applies to items in a set. So using immutable objects as elements in a set can cause problems and the behavior is undefined if changing an object affects equal comparisons.

Just as a map cannot contain itself as a key, a set can't be an element of itself although once again it'd be very bizarre program that needed to actually do that. Now the best performing implementation of a set interface is the hashset class and that uses hashes to store the items. Now this is just like a hashmap class that we've looked at. And in fact, the hashset implementation currently uses a hashmap as of java 8 although of course implementations may of course change in future versions of java.

Now if a set can be implemented using a map, then it's not hard to work out that you could actually use the corresponding map object and use only the keys ignoring the values. So this is what hashset does. And whenever an element is added to the set, it becomes a key in the underlying hashmap and a dummy object is stored as the value. So sets can be useful because operations on them are very fast. And if you're dealing with the mathematical notion of a set, then the java collection set types really allow the usual set operations such as union and intersection, which is pretty cool.

So what we're going to do is put some of this theory now into practice. We're going to create a program to model the bodies in the solar system. So in case it wasn't clear from the map lecture, I'm going to explain again how a hash collection stores objects.

Okay. So I'm just going to bring this image up on the screen now so you can see. So the essence of this is that when storing objects in a hashed collection such as hashset or hashmap think of the collection as having a number of buckets to store the objects in, you can see that represented in the graphic on the screen now. The hashcode determines which bucket an object is going to go into. Now there's a requirement that any objects that are equal should always have the same hashcode and ultimately so that they will then end up in the same bucket.

But the opposite is not required. So 2 objects that are equal do not have to have different hashcodes. So in the diagram, object one goes into bucket one, object 2 goes into bucket 2 and so on. Now object 5 has the same hashcode as object 4. So it goes into the same bucket which is bucket 4. And object 6 generates the same hashcode as object 2, so that goes into the same bucket as object 2. So when we add an object, its hash code tells the collection which bucket it should go into.

Now there may already be objects in that bucket so each is compared to the new object to make sure that it's not already in there. Now because the comparison is performed using the equals method, the collection will only know if it's already there if it's looking into the right back or looking in the right bucket. So the hashcodes must be the same and equals returns true. Now it's of no use for equals returning true if the collection is checking the wrong bucket that is if the hash code for the new object is not the same as an object that is that it's equal to.

So if we try to add another object that's equal to object, say, 6 number 6 object 6, then the hashcode will indicate that bucket 2 is the one to check. The collection class will then check all the objects in bucket 2. When it finds object 6, this will compare equal to the new object so that the new object is then not added to the collection. But on the other hand, if our new object breaks the rules and has a different hashcode to object 6, even though it compares equal to it and that's the important thing then the collection will be looking in the wrong bucket and ultimately will not find it.

So the new object will then be added to the collection and at that point we'll get a duplicate, but it can even get worse than that. So if we then iterate over the collection trying to find that new object so that we can remove it, we may we'll get to the old object 6 first and not the new one. So our code will then check if the object we've just pulled from the collection is the same that's the one we want to remove and of course equals will return true.

So we remove the object from the collection, but we've actually removed the original and not the duplicate. So we probably wouldn't iterate over the collection if we had already had a reference to the object we wanted to remove, but you can see that it's quite easy or hopefully it's easy for you to see the potential for error in this scenario. So ultimately, there has to be strict relationship between hashcode and equals. So if 2 objects compare equal, then they must have the same hash code.

So I hope that's made it clear. LECTURE 39.19: Sets Challenge Part 3
----------------------------------------

So continuing on with our challenge, our set challenge, I mentioned at the end of the previous video that there could potentially be a problem with our solar system map or I talked about so there being map issue. And the issue is with the solar system if we have a look and see how that's actually defined what we're doing is we're defining it purely with the name of the body a string and there's currently no way to cater for the body type. And obviously, because we're using a map, we've only got the concept of a key and a value. So how do we get around that.

Well, it's actually a very common problem when attempting to store and retrieve more complex objects, whether using one of the collection classes or a database for that matter and there are many solutions to this problem. Now databases allow records to be selected on several fields, so it is possible to make a primary key that consists of all the fields that uniquely define each record. Now another instance or sorry another approach is creating unique serial numbers for each record, such as a social security number for people in the US, national insurance numbers in the UK and tax file numbers in Australia.

Now one drawback of that approach is that you couldn't retrieve someone's record from a map unless you actually know their serial number. LECTURE 40.1: Exceptions
----------------------------------------

So I'm going to start off this section on input and output, io in java with an introduction to exceptions. And the reason for that is many of the methods that we'll be using to read and write files actually require that exceptions are handled. Now there's two main approaches to dealing with errors when programming. And they're often referred to as lbyl and eafp. And what that stands for is look before you leap, and easy to ask for forgiveness than permission.

So in java, it's more common to look before you leap. And we've seen this a lot when we test that an object is not null before we attempt to use it for example. Now the other approach the, eafp easy to ask for forgiveness and permission, is to go ahead and perform the operation then respond to an exception if something goes wrong. So trapping and handling exceptions is pretty simple. The code that may cause a problem is wrapped in a try block and then catch is used to deal with the exception.

Now there is a bit more to it than that things like deciding what which exceptions to catch things of that nature, but I'm going to start going through a couple of examples to demonstrate both approaches to dealing with errors and as a result of this show how exception handling is used. So I've created a new project, and let's go ahead and make a start on it and we're going to demonstrate both approaches using functions to perform integer division.

So I've got my main method here I need to write a couple of methods first so this one's going to be private static int divide, lbyl. So that's the look before you leap. So now we have so we're going to pass two integers into x and y. And we're looking before we leap.We're actually testing to see whether y is not equal to zero before we actually do any processing. So if y is not equal to zero, then we can return x divided by y. Else, we're going to return zero. So that's the look before you leap.

We're actually testing the conditions of valid because of course you can't divide something by zero, you'll actually get an error if you do that. So we're testing to make sure that the value that we're dividing by in this case y isn't zero before we actually do the test. So that's the look before you leave. Now the other way is to basically basically easy to ask for forgiveness and permission. So we're actually going to just do it a different way. So we're going to do private static int divide eafp, easy to ask for forgiveness than permission.

And that's going to be inter x in y, so same parameters but in this case we use a try block. So we type try left brace, and then we put return x divided by y. So we're not doing any testing there to see whether the values are correct. And then we need to do a catch so we've got catch. And the error we're going to catch in this case is arithmetic exception e like so, and then we just put return zero. So now that we've written our two methods, we need to call them from our main method. So we just put x equals 98 so we'll just define some values in y we're going to raise the error by making zero.

And if we do a system out print line for the look before you leap method passing x y and then we'll do it with the easy to ask for forgiveness and permission error method rather, so it's going to be divide x y. So if we run both cases or we run in both cases, you can see we've obviously got zero as a result in both scenarios so. In other words both functions can cope with an attempt to divide by zero. The lbyl method checks first that, as I mentioned, this is on line 13 return 0 if it's y 0 whereas the aafp method attempts the division and catches the exception that is raised if dividing by 0.

Now if we didn't make any attempt to cater for the possible error the program would crash and we can see that by adding another function. So we put a third function which is private static int divide into x in y. Just to confirm it does actually crash and we'll just won't do any checking and we'll actually won't add a try block either. So we'll just return x y x divided by y I should say. And then if we out put it so it's going to be just divide x y, so we should find that third method call will actually crash.

And there you go. We've actually got it to crash arithmetic exception divided by zero. So there's a lot of debate that is still going on about which method is better, but the simple answer is that really they're both better, because each approach each approach has got its own advantages that are more suited to certain situations now when using java it's more common to check first but something is you know far easier to just try and see. So in that example there's very little difference in the complexity of the two methods and I can probably you can probably have a good guess at what's going on just by reading the code.

So as I mentioned in the previous video, we're going to read in the directions.txt file that we've written, and it's a very similar process to reading the locations, but the difference is, I'm going to actually introduce a buffered reader. Now a buffered reader reads text from the input stream and buffers the characters into a character array. So for our example we're going to still create a file reader, but we're going to use it as an input stream for the buffered reader to use.

Now reading chunks of data from a stream such as a file is more efficient than reading just a few characters at a time. And the reason for that is because is that things like the overhead of seeking to the correct track and sector on the on your disk drive are significant. So it actually takes a while to find the correct place on the disk drive to read from. And if you have to do that many times because only a few bytes are being read at a time, then the seek times for this really do add up. So consequently, buffered readers can be a lot more streamlined to -- faster in other words and they're more efficient.

Now you can actually specify the size of the buffer, but the default is 8k, 8k bytes. And that's enough really for most purposes. Now our files here are both smaller than 8k. So what that means is the entire contents of the file will be read into the buffer in a single read and be available from there for the scanner to use it as it needs more data. Now this prevents excessive access to disk because the data is only read from the disk when the buffer is empty otherwise the file reader continues to take data from the memory buffer.

So it's much more optimized compared to just sort of reading a character at a time. Now you can also buffer data when it's written to disk. And not surprisingly, this makes use of a buffered writer class. The concept is the same the file writer puts data into the buffer and the data is only written to disk when the buffer is full. Now once again this prevents writing small amounts of data to the disk, which is very efficient because the disk drive generally speaking is much slower than your computer can process, so your computer application is going to be slowed down waiting for that disk drive to write data.

So by doing it this way using a buffered writer data is written in sizable chunks rather than sort of a character at a time. LECTURE 40.15: Object Input Output including Serialization
----------------------------------------

So far, we've written the locations and directions data as text as well as a binary stream. Right now we read and write each object field individually. For example, we use a read int, write int methods to read and write a location's id. And we use read utf and write utf methods to read and write a location's description. Now if an object has or had 20 fields we'd actually have to call 20 methods. So instead of that, we can use the object input stream and object output stream classes to read and write objects as a single unit.

Now when we write an object to a file, it has to be translated to a format that can be stored to a file and then reassembled into an object later when it's read by an application. Now the process of translating a data structure or object into a format that can be stored and recreated is called serialization. Now in java, when we want to use an object stream to write and read the objects of a class, we have to make the class serializable. Now we do so by making it implement the serializable interface.

Now this interface has got no methods, it's just used to give the jvm, a heads up that we may want to serialize the object to storage and to read it back again at some point. Now when we make a class serializable, it's strongly recommended that we declare a long field called serial version uid. Now if we don't do so, the compiler will give us a warning. Now this warning can usually be turned off when using an ide and unfortunately sometimes off by default and it will then calculate a default value for us.

But however, different compiler implementations may calculate different default values, and that can lead to problems down the road if we change the compiler we're using. Now there are compilers for example other than the one included with the jdk. For example, a class compiled with the standard oracle compiler for a desktop application would be compiled by a different compiler if you were to add it to an android project. So for that reason it's recommended that if we care about serialization, we actually set the serial version uid field ourselves.

So we set that value. And it's recommended that the field be private since no other class should have to use it. So what is this serial version uid field used for or think of it as a sort of a version number for the class. Now if we don't explicitly set it, the compiler will create it based on class details such as the number of fields and methods etc. And if we ever change a class, for example, by adding another field or method or change a field type, we'd have to change the serial version uid value.

When we read an object from a stream, the runtime checks the stored serial version uid against the one contained within the compiled class file. If they don't match, then there's a compatibility problem and the runtime will throw an invalid class exception. Now if we wanted later versions of an application to be able to load files created by earlier versions, we'll have to provide custom versions of the right object and read object methods by overwriting them which are methods we use to read and write objects.

So the bottom line here is that we don't have to worry about declaring a serial version uid field unless, a, we explicitly use serialization as we do when we use object input stream and the object output string classes, and b, there may be a compatibility issue down the road. But some developers and the java documentation recommend always declaring when a is true, that's when we explicitly use serialization or whether b also is true and that's there may be compatibility issues down the road. So with that theory out of the way.

Let's actually go ahead and modify our code to use the object input stream and object output stream classes. Our first step is to make the location class serializable by having it implement the serializable interface. Let's go and have a look at that. So will that be serialized when a location object is written to a file. Well, in our case it will be because linked hash map implements the serializable interface. So we're actually lucky. When we write a location object, the entire contents of the exits field will also be serialized.

Now if linked hashmap didn't implement serializable, we'd actually be responsible for writing the code to store its content to the file ourselves. Now ideally, when we want an object to be serializable, all its fields will also be serializable. So you have to keep that in mind when writing your own classes. If a class we want to serialize will have fields from other classes that you write, then you need to make sure those other classes are serializable as well.

Well, the answer is it'll only contain one. Since both few instances refer to the same bar instance, only one bar instance is serialized. So in other words a serialized file will only ever contain one copy of the same instance.

So that's pretty cool. But now imagine that we want to do the same thing, but for some reason we want to create two files. So we write both few instances to file one and then both to file two. So how many instances of bar will be written this time. Well, the answer in that case is two. Object instances will be unique within a file, but not across files. So in this case when the two files are read back into an application, two distinct instances of bar would be created.

Now this may not matter, but it could which is why it's important to understand that that can happen in this case. Of course, in the two file case there could also be two instances of each flu object read back in as well. All right. So to close the section on the java.io package. We're going to take a look at the java.io.random access file class. Now so far we've been reading and writing files sequentially, we start at byte 0 and we read and write and we read or write bytes one after the other until we reach the end of file or until we finish writing the data. So we don't jump around in the file in other words.

For example, we don't read bytes 20 to 35 in the file and then read bytes 50 to 100 and then bytes 10 to 15. And likewise, we don't write out bytes 100 to 150 and then bytes 20 to 30. Now the file pointer is an offset in the file where the next read or write will start from. Now for example if the file pointer is set to 100, then the next time we call a read or write method the read or write will start at byte position 100 in the file. Now if we're reading an int the byte set positions 100 to 103 would be red since an int is 4 bytes.

The byte position is zero based. So the first byte in the file is at position zero. Whenever we read or write the file, the file pointer is advanced by the number of bytes we read or wrote. So for example if the file pointer is equal to 100 and we read 5 bytes, then the file pointer will be equal to 105 after the read write has taken place. Now also we use the term offset when randomly accessing files. So an offset is a byte location in the file.

So for example if the value has an offset of 100, that would mean that the value is located at byte 100 in the file so we'd want the file pointer to be set to 100 when we read write the value. Now the value could of course occupy more than one byte but the offset is where the whether the values first byte is located. The remaining bytes would follow that first byte sequentially. In java 1.4, a new io package was added to the java software development kit. Now they called it java.nio and the package was described back then as an improvement to java io and that's because the classes in the package perform io in a non-blocking manner. Now java nio was also meant to fix some of the inherent problems developers could run into when using the java.io classes to work with the file system. Now the java.no class has fall into one of two buckets those that deal with the file system and also those that deal with reading and writing data.

In this video, we're going to start looking at the classes that read data from and write data to a data source. Now when using classes in the java.io package, a thread will block while it's waiting to read or write to a stream or buffer. However, threads using the java.nio class or classes will not block. In other words, they're free to continue executing. And consequently, you could really say that java.nio was introduced as a performance improvement.

That said, many developers have argued that the java.nio package was a step backwards. And in fact there's examples on the internet that people have shown that blocking io which is in the java.io package is often faster than the non-blocking io in the java.no package. And the discussion on threads and blocking etc is covered in the thread section of the course by the way just in case you haven't seen that section of the course yet and wondering what that's all about.

Now also working with the java.nio class is more complex and you'll see that when we go through to start writing some code. Now as has happened with other additions to the java language, many developers still prefer to write code using the older java.io classes, and you may very well decide to do that as well. But I do feel it's important to understand the new way of doing io with the java.nio package just in case you're ever asked to work with code that uses it.

Now previously you learnt that the java.io classes work with streams that is character and binary. Now data is read one vital character at a time and sometimes buffered depending on which classes are used. Now when using java.nio however you'll deal with data in blocks. And rather than processing a single byte or character at a time, one block will be processed at a time. Now to accomplish this you'll need to use channels and buffers and you'll see what they are and how to use those in later videos in this section in the course.

So with all that said about java.nio, you can use java.nio methods to create a java.io stream. But more on that later. LECTURE 40.22: Reading and Writing with Java NIO
----------------------------------------

All right. So in the last video, we finished working with java.nio and java.io. So in other words we're getting the java.nio classes to create commonly used java.io streams. It's now time to take a look at how to read and write text files using java.nio only. Now I said that doing io using java.nio means that datum is processed in blocks rather than one byte or character at a time. And to accomplish this java.nio uses channels and buffers and also sometimes selectors so in terms of definitions a channel is the data source you're reading from or writing to.

Now that can be a file a socket or any other data source. Now to use a data source as a channel, you need a class that implements the java.nio.channel interface and that can connect to the data source. Now a buffer on the other hand is the container for the block of data that you want to read or write. Now buffers are typed that means that they can only hold one type of data, and you can actually specify the size of the buffer as well. And finally, selectors. Well, they allow a single thread to manage the IO for multiple channels.

Now we won't actually be covering selectors because they're really generally only needed to enlarge enterprise applications. Now when working with streams, which if you recall can be byte based or character based and we saw that in previous videos, you need two instances of a java.io class if you want to both read and write a file. LECTURE 40.29: Filesystem
----------------------------------------

So far you've learned how to create, read and write files and data sources using java.nio. Now sometimes you don't want to read from a file or write to a file. You may want to copy files, delete files, move them so on and so forth. In other words, you want to work with the file system. In this case, java.nio has you covered. In fact, there's a whole package dedicated to working with the file system called java.nio.file. So what we're going to do is start by taking a look at the path interface which is what you use to identify a file on the file system.

Now we've already used paths previously in this section of the course. If you recall, we created them when we wanted to use java.io classes to read and write files, but we called them methods such as files.new buffer writer so that the buffered writer would be backed by a java.nio buffer and channel. So what actually is a path. Well, no doubt you're familiar with the concept of a file path because you use them all the time. Now if you open the file explorer on your system, you'll see a bunch of root folders, usually hard drives, peripheral drives like DVD or blu-ray drives, external drives thumb drives etc.

Each of these top level drives is a root node in a path. For example, on windows, the directory c column backslash is the root node for the c drive. Now each folder, which is also referred to as a directory is also a node in a path. And then of course there's the file itself. Now if you've downloaded a file and placed it in the c colon backslash downloads directory, again, on windows, then the file path has three nodes. One for c column backslash, one for the downloads directory and then one for the file itself.

So this path is unique. You can't have two files with the same name in the same directory because each file is identified by its path. For the downloads example if you named the file you downloaded data.txt, then the path would be c column backslash downloads backslash file.txt, again on windows. So you wouldn't be able to place a second file called file.txt into that same directory. So the character used to separate the directory names in a path is called the delimiter, and it can differ between operating systems.

For example, in windows, the delimiter is the backslash. But on unix and mac, the delimiter is the forward slash. So everything we discuss about paths applies to files and directories. To keep things simple, we won't always refer to both, but you can create a path for a file or a directory. Now sometimes it won't make sense to use a path to a directory for example when you want to create a file. But other times it'll only make sense to use a path to a directory.

It will depend on what you want to do. So just keep in mind that paths can refer to either a file or a directory. Now file paths can be absolute or relative. So the path c colon backslash downloads backslash file.txt. Well, that's an absolute path because it starts at a root node, but the path photos backslash vacation backslash mountain.jpg, well, that's a relative path because it doesn't specify a root node at the start. In other words, it doesn't contain enough information to identify the file.

So in other words, you'll have to be combined with another path that does contain a root node. Now when using relative paths in applications there's usually the concept of a current or working directory that you can combine with a relative path. For example, when you were running applications that used path, we didn't specify the entire path. We did something like the following on the next slide. You can see there we did we didn't actually specify the root node so the string data.txt in that code example doesn't give enough information about where the file is located.

But you'll notice that we're calling the filesystems.getdefault method first and then the getpath method. So what's happening here is that the getdefault method call returns a file system object with a working directory set to the current user directory. So when running an application from within intellij, the current user directory is the intellij project directory, and so that's the working directory for the file system object. Now the working directory is then combined with the path that you pass to the get path call and that's why the files are created then in the intellij projects directory.

So instead of what we did in the previous example, we could have done something similar to what you can see on the screen there now, and we've got two backslashes there because we're using a backslash we have to escape that so that java actually knows we're referring to a backslash. But the point is here though we could have changed the scenario in these paths and then called the dot get method with an absolute path call instead of what we did in the previous example.

But notice here that we're using the paths class which has got an s at the end when we call the get method. All right, so now that you've got an idea on how to build paths to files in the current directory in a path relative to another directory or to anywhere around the file system using an absolute path, let's now briefly discuss why the path interface came about. So the java.io file class also points to files on the file system.

So why did the java developers introduce another class that effectively does the same thing in java 7. So the file class more useful though has a few problems. And specifically, those problems are firstly, many methods in that class don't throw exceptions or don't provide specific error messages when they fail. An example would be the file.delete method which returns a boolean. And if the deletion fails, you can't actually tell if it was because the file didn't exist or the application doesn't have permission to delete the file or some other reason.

So unfortunately, the method doesn't provide that level of information. Now the file.rename method works differently on different platforms. And java is supposed to be portable as across platforms meaning that the code shouldn't have to worry about which operating system it's running on. Another problem there's no support for symbolic links. And a symbolic link is a kind of file that points to another file sort of like a shortcut in windows if you're familiar with that.

Now they're often used with networks to point to a remote location. Unfortunately, the file class doesn't understand those symbolic links. The file class doesn't provide a way to get metadata about a file information such as permissions, its owner or other security information. The metadata that it does provide is retrieved inefficiently as well. Now many of the methods don't perform well when working with lots of data. For example, if you use the file class to request a list of all the files in the directory and there are a lot of files the method can actually hang believe it or not.

And lastly, the last error since the file class doesn't understand symbolic links walking through a directory tree is therefore problematic. So we'll end the video here in the next video, let's have a talk about how java.nio solves these problems and also how it splits the functionality that was in the file class into several different classes and interfaces. See you in the next video.

LECTURE 40.36: Walk File Tree
----------------------------------------

All right, we're ready to start learning how to walk a file tree. Now again when I talk about walking or fall tree, what I mean is that we're going to visit every file and directory that can be reached from a starting or root directory for that tree. For example, if we started in dir2 in the dir2 folder in our project, we'll visit the following files and directories, but again not necessarily in this order. So it'd be the dir2 folder. And within the dir2 folder, we've got the files, file1, file2 and file 3, 2.txt files1, dat file.

But then also we'll have the dir3 folder. We'll go into that subfolder as well and also the two files in there, file1.txt and file2.txt. So in this scenario because we're going to be starting on the dir2 folder, well that's considered to be the root of its file tree. So we're never going to move up a level from the root directory, we're only going to be moving down levels. Now you might be wondering why would you actually want to do this. Well, one use case might be when the application has to find a file.

But another use case could be that the application is searching all the files in the directory and below for a specific string. Now I mentioned in a previous video that when you want to copy a directory, you have to walk the file tree if you want to copy everything below it as well. Otherwise, only the files directly within the directory itself will be copied. ----------------------------------------
LECTURE 42.2: Database Terminology
----------------------------------------

So let's go through some common database terminology that should be useful for you when we're working with the databases in this section of the course. And the idea here is that it will make it a lot easier to understand the app when you understand what the fundamentals are and what all the actual various terms mean. Now at the very basic level, the database is the container for all the data that you store or that resides inside it. Now when you use the term database you're referring to the entire data as well as the structure, it's actually stored in and in addition any queries and views on that data.

Now in SQLite, the entire database contents are stored in one single file. But that isn't true of most large database systems. Now the database dictionary provides a comprehensive list of the structures and types of data that are used in recording the data. So, it basically describes all the tables and fields within the database. Now more on the specifics later, but in SQLite, there is a table in each database called sql_lite_master that has this information in it.

Now you can query that table but there are commands that do it for you, so you don't have to understand the structure of the master table. But it's there for you anyway and as we go through you will see how these commands actually work. Now a table is a collection of related data held in a database. So think of a contact database for example that stores the name and the address and the phone number of perhaps your customers or what about an invoice table, that records the invoice number and details of the invoice.

So in this slide, there are two tables contacts and invoices that are used to store information about contacts and invoice details. Now with SQLite databases such as SQLite or another database like Microsoft SQL server, they're ideal for storing structured data that can be organized neatly into rows and columns, like you can see in these examples. Now with all the interest in big data, there are now databases such as NoSQL or Hadoop, that can cope with data that doesn't have such an obvious structure, but we're going to be restricting our use of database to structured data.

So a field is the basic unit of data in a table. So a field in a database can be thought of probably in a similar way to what a variable is and you've seen those obviously. And just like a class variable, a database field has a name and a type. Now the type restricts what kind of data can be stored in a field. For example, it could be a string or it could accept numbers. Now many databases also allow date fields, large text fields, and also fields where you can store things like photographs or audio.

And these field types are often called blobs, which is supposed to stand for binary large object. It's a great name and I can't help thinking that the original acronym was something like LBO for large binary object and they came up with a cooler-sounding name afterwards. Now fields are often referred to as columns in databases. I know this can be technically confusing sometimes because if you come from an excel background, you'll find that the definition is probably a bit different to what you think of as a column.

Now, in a spreadsheet, the term column refers to an entire set of data extending across many rows. But in a relational database, column generally refers to a single entry. Although, when talking about the structure of a table rather than the actual data, then you could talk about a column to hold the invoice number, which is probably closer to the spreadsheet use of the term. Now when referring to the data in the database though, we're talking about an individual item like a base unit of data.

Now relational databases existed nearly 10 years before the first spreadsheet program and we just have to accept that column means slightly different things in each case, but more on that shortly. Now a row or record is a single set of data for all fields that are in that table. So if you've got four columns like the example on the screen and if your table has an invoice number or a date, a description, and an amount, then a row represents those four values for a single invoice.

So it's really a collection of all the columns that comprise the details of one entry in that table. So the highlighted record holds the details for invoice number 2, which was a laptop costing just over a thousand dollars sold on the 24th of May, 2016. And you can use either of the terms row or record to identify it, but the correct relational database terminology is actually row. Now a flat file database stores all the data in a single file, which can result in a lot of duplication of data.Now here, ISP's credit limit needs to be increased, so that they can purchase the monitor as otherwise, they actually go over the limit.

So in order to increase the limit, the data in three rows would have to be modified. Now as you can see, every row in the table that contains a record for ISP must be changed in order to increase the credit limit. So flat file databases are not used very often anymore, but they were fairly popular in the early days as they directly mapped to those card index record that companies sometimes used. Now if we were storing names, addresses, and phone number type information, then a flat file database is fine for the job and even today, people still use address books and rolex style contact systems with each person's details on a different card.

But there isn't really much need to relate the individual cards to each other, this works perfectly well. Now as you can see from this invoice example though trying to store all the data in a single table results in duplicate data. results in duplicate data. can be related to other tables which is very useful. So continuing on with the invoice example, we can split the data out into a customer table, which contains standard company data such as their name, address, and a credit limit.

And another table called invoices containing all that customers’ purchases. The name column in the customer table is related to the name column in the invoices table. Now in relational database terms, this is called a join. In fact, in this example we have a one too many join because there can and there probably will be many invoice rows for each customer using a relational model, updating a customer's credit limit involves changing the data in just a single row.

So there is a mechanism to join these two tables to link the individual records in each table to each other. And you'll often see designs where a third table is used to provide the link as in this next slide. And it's also very common to use a linking table to relate the data to two other tables. Now here when an invoice record is stored, a new record is created in the Customer_Invoices table to link, for example, invoice triple 004 with customer ISP.

Now one advantage of this is that the invoice table only contains data relating to invoices. The rows are not cluttered up with customer information of any kind, not even the customer name. Splitting the data up like this is known as normalization. Now database normalization is basically the process of removing redundant, duplicated, and irrelevant data from the tables, and the more that this is done, the higher the level of normalization. If you look into normalization, you'll find that you can go up to level six, six normal form, but in most practical applications, it's rare to go beyond the third level.

Now it's an interesting subject but the math can get a bit horrible at the higher levels. Our example on the slide isn't quite as normal as we should be because we've used the customer name as the link between the customer and invoice tables. Now if one of our customers changed its name which is quite a common thing to happen, then we have to update each of the relevant entries in the Customer_Invoices table as well. Now the usual way to deal with this is to use a unique ID field, that stays the same for each customer once it's allocated.

Now we shouldn't store the customer balances in the table as that's best calculated when needed. So a view is a way of looking at the data, in a format similar to a table but bringing data together from more than one joined table. So in this example, the view contains columns from the customer table and the invoices table. So if you can just contain just some columns from a single table, for example, just the description column from the invoices table to produce a list of items that have been sold.

Now in SQLite, the data in a view can't be updated. So that means that you can't add a new row to a view and have it place the new data into the relevant tables. Now some databases such as Microsoft SQL Server do allow this, but in that case, the views do have restrictions on the columns that can and must contain if they're used in this way. So that's not something we need to worry about because we can't do that in SQLite. All right, so that's enough to get us started and we're going to explore these terms more as we go through SQLite.

So coming up in the next videos, we're going to discuss a few more database concepts and I'll be going into more detail. We'll be using practical examples and actually using the SQLite database. Now the major client server databases have what are known as stored procedures, which are a way to store SQL queries amongst other things and execute them when you want, often with parameters for things like the text to search for.

They operate a little bit like functions or methods that are stored in the database and can be reused when you want. Unfortunately, though SQLite doesn't have stored procedures. And there's actually a good reason for this. And it's a result of the fact that SQLite is intended to be embedded in programs. So normal client service SQL databases have the database server running on a remote machine that you connect to in order to access the data. A stored procedure runs on the server so it's far more efficient than trying to work with a large data set on a remote machine.

But as SQL lite is not client server and everything is running on the same machine anyway, the advantages of using stored procedures really don't apply. In addition, you don't generally use SQLite interactively like we're doing here. We're doing this because we develop applications and need to try things out and get queries working etc. but ordinary users wouldn't normally interact with a SQL database in this way, it would all be done by the application itself.

The bottom line here is the absence of stored procedures isn't really a drawback when you consider the way in which SQLite is intended to be used. But one thing that it does have in common with the client server database systems is views. So a good way to think about a view is as a virtual table. So you can't update, delete or insert, but you can query them just as if they were a table.

So we've seen how to work with a SQLite database from the command line. Now we're going to learn how to use a database from a java application. And to do so, we're going to be using the JDBC API. Now JDBC stands for java database connectivity. So using JDBC, we can not only work with databases, but also spreadsheets and flat files. So think of JDBC as a middleman that sits between a java application and a data source. To use a particular data source from an application, we need the JDBC driver for the data source.

For example, to access a SQLite database from an application, we need a SQLite JDBC driver. Now the driver is simply a java library containing classes that implement the JDBC API. Now because all JDBC drivers have to implement the same interfaces, it's not difficult to change the data source and application users. For example, if an application uses a SQLite database and then we decide later that we want to use a MySQL database, all we have to do is use the MySQL JDBC driver instead of the SQLite one in addition to of course migrating the data to a MySQL database.

Now in reality, unfortunately, it's not that simple. Nothing is ever 100 portable. But if we write our JDBC code with thought in mind that we may have to change the data source later, we can make our lives easier by avoiding the use of database specific SQL code and also behaviors wherever possible. If we wanted to work with a spreadsheet or a flat file that's fine as long as there's a JDBC driver that works with that spreadsheet or file format.

And if you're feeling particularly a game, you can always write the JDBC driver yourself if necessary. Now the JDBC driver has to be written in java but it can consist of a thin java layer that calls code written in other languages. So the current version of the JDBC API as of shooting this video is JDBC 4.2. For backwards compatibility, it contains all the methods that were in previous JDBC versions. Now there have been changes to the way that JDBC works.

So make sure you're working with a driver that supports the at least JDBC 4.0. And if you use the one, we'll download in this video, you'll be fine. JDBC consists of two packages, java dot SQL which is core JDBC and java x dot SQL which is optional JDBC. Now the APIs in the java x dot SQL package are required when working with database servers. And we'll talk about those a little bit later. Now all the popular databases provide JDBC drivers. Now every result set has a cursor. Now this cursor isn't the same as a database cursor. We could have had several result set objects and each one will have a cursor. However, and this is actually quite important, if we re-use a statement object to do a query, then any result set associated with that statement object is closed and a new one is created for the new query. So if we want to work with several query results at the same time then it's imperative to use a different statement instance for each query.

Reusing the statement instance was okay when we were just doing insertions updates and deletes because we weren't using or checking the result. Now we can reuse the statement object to query but only if we finish processing the results of one query before we execute the next query. And keep in mind that a statement object ultimately can only ever have one active result set associated with it. Now when a result set is created its cursor is positioned before the first record.

And so the first time we call results dot next, the cursor will be moved to the first record. Now when we call it again, the cursor will be moved to the second record in the result set when there's no more records. The next method will return false. And when we call one of the results sets get methods, the values returned are those from the record at the result set's cursor's current position. Now we'll come back to the result set cursor where we work with a database from within a GUI application.

Now note that result set is a resource. So we have to close it. And you can see that I added the results dot close on line 35. And that's because it's associated with the statement instance. We have to close it before we close the statement. Now we're closing all our resources at the end of the try block. If an exception is thrown, it's possible that the closed methods won't be executed. Even though some or all other resources have been created.

Now for our small application it doesn't matter. When the database objects are destroyed, they'll do the appropriate. Cleanup the close method forces the closing of the database. Resource immediately rather than waiting for them to be automatically closed. Because of that we don't have to close them ourselves but it's actually good practice to do so. And if our code belonged to a large application which there were lots of open connections and result sets and statements, we'd have to be a lot more diligent about making sure the resources were closed as soon as we no longer needed them.

Let's just press enter there. And you can see what happened there. Suddenly, we've got every row in the artist underscore list view being returned to us. You can right up to the top again. And you can see what's happened with the SQL code there where title equals go your own way, or one equals one or double quote double quote. So what we've done, we've just performed what's known as a SQL injection attack. Now in this particular case, perhaps it doesn't matter if a user gets to see all the songs in a view, but what happens if this was a view or table of user ids and passwords for example or worse still it contained credit card details or rather sensitive financial or even medical information.

So that wouldn't be a good thing. So how did this actually happen. Well, the thing was when we built the SQL statement, we blindly concatenating whatever the users typed. So when we entered the above string, the code built the following SQL statement which I've just mentioned here. So select name album track from artist underscore list where title equals go your own way in double quotes or one equals one or and then two double quotes. Now since one equals one will be true for every record, all the records in the artist underscore list view are returned.

So this is called a SQL injection attack because a user has injected SQL into the statement that we didn't intend to run. Now the user in this scenario would usually be a hacker, and they try this because they know something about how applications that use databases are coded. They guess that we could be concatenating the name into a where clause as we're doing here. And since it's a string, they guess that we're concatenating a closing quote which is why they end their input string with a quote.

Now a malicious user can even do something like drop tables. Since we're using JDBC, we do have some protection against that. At least when using the SQLite JDBC driver, the execute and execute query methods won't run more than a single SQL statement. So in other words a user can't tack on something like semicolon drop table songs. But if an application written in a language like perhaps php was running SQL directly based on user input rather than going through an API, then a malicious user would be able to execute whatever SQL statements they wanted.

So instead of building up query strings and using the statement class to execute them, we should really be using the prepared statement class. Now prepared statements can protect against SQL injection attacks because when we use them, we don't concatenate user input into the SQL statement that will ultimately be running. So let's look at an example. Now as I've noted the only thing that changes between queries is the song title. Now I mentioned in a previous video that it would be nice if we could have placeholders in SQL statements for the values that change from query to query.

And prepared statements allow us to do just that. So let's go back to our data source class. And we're going to add a constant at the top of the class. We'll start down here on line 88. That's going to be PSFS, and it's going to be query underscore view underscore song underscore info underscore prep is equal to. Then the word from in double quotes with a space to start at the end plus our table underscore artist underscore song view plus that aware space around the space to the left and right plus column underscore song underscore title plus equals, and this time I'm adding a question mark there. So the only difference here between this constant and the one we used before is that we're using a question mark for the song title.

So this is the placeholder character that we use in prepared statements. When we're ready to perform the query, we'll replace the placeholder with the actual title we want to query. So the SQL statement we're building is select name album track from artists underscore list where title equals question. That's ultimately what we're actually creating with this constant on the line above. So note that importantly we don't put quotation marks around the song title.

When replacing a placeholder in a prepared statement, the database actually understands that a string like go your own way is one value. So we only substitute a single value for each placeholder. Now since there's no song on the database with the title go your own way or one equals one or double quote, no records were returned.
