Okay. So continuing on from the last video, we ended up talking about the fact that a malicious user can't inject SQL into the statement. And that's because anything substituted for a placeholder is treated as a single literal value and won't be interpreted as SQL. But moving on from that, let's say that we wanted to use or within a prepared statement. How do we do that? And what I'm talking about is some SQL code along these lines. So select name album track from artist, what's called list, where title equals question mark or artist equals question mark.

So think of it this way. For each value, we need a placeholder. We can't substitute more than one value for one placeholder, and we can't inject SQL. And also, we can only substitute values. So we can't use placeholders for things like table and column names. And that's because in order to pre-compile the statements, the database needs to know which table we're querying and which columns we want. So the only information we can postpone until we want to perform the query are the values themselves.

Also, we can use prepared statements with insert, update and delete. We use placeholders for the values in the same way we'd use them within select statements. And we'll actually see an example of using a search shortly. So it is good practice to use prepared statements because of the potential performance benefit and also because they protect the database against SQL injection attacks. Now of course that doesn't mean that our database can't be hacked, but just that it cannot be hacked using that particular type of attack.

So to recap, we do the following to use a prepared statement. We declare a constant for the SQL statement that contains the placeholders. We create a prepared statement instance using connection dot prepare statement, and we pass that the SQL statement in a string. When we're ready to perform the query or the insert update or delete, we call the appropriate set of methods to set the placeholders to the values we want to use in the statement. We then run the statement using prepared statement dot execute or prepared statement dot execute query.

Lastly, we process the results the same way we do when using a regular old statement. So that's all for prepared statements. Our final topic for this particular video is going to be transactions. Now because the JDBC connection class auto commits changes by default, every time we call execute to insert, update or delete records. Those changes are saved to the database as soon as the SQL statement completes. Now sometimes that's what we want. But too often, it's not.

As an example, let's just say that our application is a web portal that people use to do online banking. Now one of the things that they can do is transfer money from one account to another. When they do this, we have to run two SQL statements. The first one we need to update the source account with the new balance. And the second one is to update the destination account with the new balance. Now what would happen if we executed the first statement successfully, but the second statement failed for some reason.

So let's say the source account had a balance of 1000 dollars and the destination account had a balance of 100 dollars. And the customer wants to transfer $200 into the destination account. Now in step 1, we update the record for the source account so that it now has a balance of 800. In step 2, we update the destination account so that it has a balance of 300. Now step one completes, but step two fails the 200 dollars we're transferring will effectively go missing.

Now hopefully we'd notice the failure, but then we'd have to write code that would handle any failures by adding the money back to the source account. But what happens if we can't do that because the second step failed because the database is down, or it can't be reached. What do we do then? And here's another scenario. Let's suppose we want to add a new song to the music database. What do we have to do to achieve this? Firstly, we want to add the artist for the song to the artists table.

Secondly, we want to add the album the song is on to the albums table. And third, we want to add the song to the songs table. But what happens if we complete step one but then steps two and three keep failing? You know maybe we're trying to do this over the internet, and we lose our internet connection for some reason. Now this wouldn't be as bad a situation as the banking example, but we would end up with records in the artists and or albums table that aren't associated with any songs.

The integrity of the data in the database could be compromised. So it would be nice if when we wanted to accomplish something that requires multiple SQL statements, we could run all the statements as a single unit. So either all the SQL statements would successfully complete or none of them would. Now this is where transactions come in. So think of a transaction as a sequence of SQL statements that are treated as a single logical unit. Now if any of the statements fail, the results of any previous statements in the transaction can be rolled back or just not saved.

It's as if they never happened. Now in the banking case, if step two failed, then the balance in the source account would be rolled back to its original value. In the music case, if steps one and two are successful, but step three fails then step one and two are rolled back. So the artist and album are never saved in the artists and albums tables. Note that when we're speaking about databases, we usually use the term commit rather than save when referring to making any changes permanent.

So we use commit from this point forward. Now database transactions must be acid compliant. They must meet the following characteristics. So the a in asset stands for atomicity. Now this relates to what we've just discussed. If a series of SQL statements change the database, then either all the changes are committed or none of them are. The second letter c stands for consistency. Before a transaction begins, the database is in a valid state. When it completes, the database is still in a valid state.

The i in asset stands for isolation. So until the changes committed by a transaction are completed, they won't be visible to other connections. So transactions can't depend on each other. And lastly, the d in asset stands for durability. Once the changes performed by transaction are committed to the database, they're permanent. Now if an application then crashes or the database server goes down in the case of a client server database like MySQL for example.

The changes made by the transactions are still there when the application runs again, or the database comes back up. So essentially, transactions ensure the integrity of the data within a database. Now we only have to use transactions when we change the data in a database. We don't need them if we're querying the database since we're not changing any data. SQLite uses transactions by default and auto commits by default. In fact, no changes can be made to the database outside of transaction.

So when we were working with the contacts database, every time we used update, insert and delete, SQLite was creating a transaction running the statement and then committing the changes for us. So as we learned earlier the JDBC connection class also auto commits changes by default. When we turned off auto commit, SQLite stopped auto committing the changes, but they were still made as part of a transaction. Now when working with SQLite, the following commands are used for transactions.

Firstly, begin transaction. Now we use this to manually start a transaction. The second one is end transaction. So we use this to end the transaction. Now committing changes automatically ends a transaction. Also, ending a transaction also commits any changes. So in other words, end transaction and commit are aliases. We only have to use one when we want to enter transaction and commit the changes. Three commit. So we use this to commit the changes made by a transaction.

As mentioned, this enters the transaction, so we don't need to also run the end transaction command. Four, roll back. So this rolls back any uncommitted changes and ends the transaction. So note that it can only roll back changes that have occurred since the last commit or rollback. Note that if we close a connection before we commit any outstanding changes, the changes are rolled back. All right. So let's take a look at how to use transactions within JDBC.

Now when using JDBC, we don't code the transaction related SQL statements and use statement objects to execute them. What we do instead is call methods in the connection class to execute transaction related commands. So we can perform the following steps. Firstly, turn off the default auto commit behavior by calling dot set auto commit with false as an argument. Two, we perform the SQL operations that form the transaction. Three, if there are no errors call connection dot commit to commit the changes.

And if there are errors, we call connection dot rollback to rollback any changes made since the transaction began. And number four, we turn the default auto commit behavior back on by calling set auto commit this time passing true as the argument. So to demonstrate a transaction, we're going to add the code to insert a song into the songs table. All right. So at the end of the last video, we created -- we ended up finishing off the insert song method. So let's now just go through what we've actually done here. So we start over here by starting a transaction and we do that by turning off the auto commit behavior of the connection. Now the default behavior you may recall is to commit every change. And the way the database does that is by running every update delete and insert statement as a transaction.

Now when we want to run a series of SQL statements as a transaction, we signal that by turning off the default behavior. From that point forward, we're actually in a new transaction. So after calling set auto commit here to turn off the default behavior and starting a new transaction, we perform all the actions we have to take to insert a song. So we start off by inserting the artist and then we insert the album using the artist id that was returned from the insert artist method.

Once we get to that point, we can now insert the song. Now we do that by setting the values and insert into a song's prepared statement, these three lines here. And then we actually call the execute update to check that only one row was affected. And that's the row that was added for the song. Now if that's the case, we're actually done. We've inserted the song and all its associated information. So we want to commit the changes, and we're doing that on this line.

And once we've done that that also ends the transaction. Now if something goes wrong and an exception is thrown, we're calling this connection dot rollback down here. And that's going to back out any changes we've made since starting the transaction. And it will also end the transaction. And finally, down here in the finally block, we're actually setting the set order commit method or calling it with the value of true to return to the default auto commit behavior.

Now because using transactions involves getting database locks, it's best practice to only turn off auto commit for the duration of a transaction and to turn it back on again immediately afterwards. Once it's turned back on unless we turn it off again, any insert updates or deletes will be auto committed as soon as they've completed. Now resetting the default behavior in the finally block ensures that it will be done whether the transaction succeeds but also if it fails.

So hopefully, now at this point you can see why we have the insert artist and insert album methods both through the SQL exception rather than handling it. If you recall both of these methods we're throwing the SQL exception, and we're also in the two cases here where there's a problem with inserting or there's a problem with the generator keys, we're throwing the exceptions the SQL exception there. And likewise for the insert album. So that's why these methods aren't handling the SQL exceptions. We're just throwing back to the insert song method where these are ultimately called from so what it means is that all the code that makes up the transaction is actually now in one block and quite easy to read.So it's really just this block here that's updating potentially the three tables.

So we use them when we want to perform a series of SQL statements as a unit, so that the changes are only committed to the database if all the statements run successfully.

If a statement fails or something else happens, perhaps the lost connection or the database server goes down in the middle of performing a transaction, then we won't end up with a database in an invalid state. We'll be able to roll back any changes that have been made or if the connection goes down for some reason, the database will automatically roll back any changes and end the transaction. Now one final note here, it's also possible to roll back a transaction to a specific point rather than rolling back all the changes that have been made since the transaction started.

So to do this, all we need to do is call the connection dot set save point method, which returns a save point object. If we need to roll back the changes that have been made since we created the save point, we pass the save point to the connection dot rollback method. So in other words, we do a connection dot rollback then we pass that save point object. But we'd only do this where it makes sense to roll back any part of a transaction when something goes wrong. All Right. So the last video we finished off queries and we've got our application working okay, but how about inserts updates and deletes of data. How do we go about doing that given that we really only worked on queries today? So we do handle them the same way, but the question is how and when do we update the user interface. Usually, we'll already be displaying data and the user will do something they'll add a new record, update a record or delete a record though they won't think of it that way.

In our case, they'd want to update an artist name perhaps to correct a spelling error or delete an artist because they gave away the only album they had by that artist, or they want to add a new album which could result in also adding a new record to the artist's table. So we want to keep the database and the UI in sync. Now there are a couple of ways to do this. The first is to re-query the database after every successful insert, update and delete.

And when working with a small data set like the artists table that's okay, but for larger data sets it may not make sense. Now this is one area where it will depend on the databases and application you're working on. So another alternative would be to perform the database operation and then manually update the user interface. We wouldn't re-query the database. In our case, when doing an insert, we get the list the table view is displaying and add the new artist record.

And because we're using data binding, when we add the new record to the list, it would then automatically be displayed in the table. So that was for an insert. For an update, we'd get the list the table view is displaying find the record and update the field. Once again, because of data binding, the change will be reflected in the table. And lastly, for a delete, same dealers insert except I would actually delete the record. So we'll update the user interface after the database operation has successfully completed.

Now if something is going to go wrong, it's more likely that the database operation will fail. So we don't want to update the user interface first. Because if the database operation fails, the user interface will be out of sync with the database. But if the database operation succeeds, but for some reason the user interface update fails, that's not really as bad. The user won't see the change, but most likely there'll be a refresh button either in our application or on the browser they're using if they're using a web application.

Worst case though they'd have to manually refresh the data to see the change just as we sometimes have to do that when using this SQLite browser and they'd only have to do this if the user interface update failed and that would probably be pretty rare. LECTURE 43.1: Networking Overview
----------------------------------------

In this video, we're going to start learning about java networking. Now firstly, we're going to start off with some terminology just to make sure that you're on the same page. Now a network is a system of computers connected together so that they can share resources and communicate with each other. Now networking refers to how the connected computers communicate. Now when using java, the java.net package contains the classes you generally want to use to establish connections between computers and then send messages between those computers.

Now when writing a networking code, you need to be familiar with threads and input output streams, and I've covered those in other sections of this course already. So if you haven't watched those sections, I suggest you do that before moving on with networking in this section. Now these days networking is usually discussed in the context of the internet, but computers may also communicate across a private network also known as an intranet. In fact, that's where networking actually began and intranets are still common today in business.

For example, office computers don't usually have a printer at their desks, they share a printer. When they print a file or document, the document is sent to the printer over the business's intranet. Now sometimes a single business will have multiple intranets one for each department. Most software teams use version control meaning that developers have to check files into a central repository and other developers can then check out the files and work on them.

Now some teams use version control applications available in the cloud such as GitHub, but others use version control that's in-house running on the business's intranet. Unless you'll see you can also use networking when you want applications running on the same machine to communicate with each other. So networking can be involved even when only one machine is involved. But let's stop saying machine. When discussing networking, a machine is usually referred to as a host.

Now a common networking configuration that you've probably heard of is client server, meaning that one or more hosts on the network are acting as servers and the other hosts are clients that connect to the server. Now at a high level that's how the internet operates. The browser is the client. And when you type in a web address, it connects to the server that has the files for the website at that address. Now of course that's overly simplified, but essentially that's how the internet works.

Now as I mentioned, you can have a client server interaction on the same host. For example, the MySQL database comes with software called workbench that you can use to perform database operations. So the workbench is the client and it connects to the MySQL database server on that local host. But of course, it can also connect remotely to another server if needed as well. Now another example is local web development. It's possible to run an Apache or IIS web server on your computer and connect to it using a browser on that same computer.

And in fact, that's often what web developers do when they're working on a website for a client. So computers on a network which includes the internet communicate with each other using a transport protocol. Now we'll use the TCP and UDP protocols moving forward in this section. Now generally a computer will have one physical connection to a network. And anything sent to the computer from other hosts on the network will arrive through that connection.

But sometimes the same computer will be running multiple applications that want data from the network. For example, at any one time, you might have a browser open, a chat application open and you might be streaming music and so on and so forth. So when data arrives at the one physical connection to the network, how does it get routed to the target application. Well, that's where ports come in. Each application that needs data from the network is assigned a port, and this includes clients connecting to a server that's on the same machine.

And when data arrives, the port number is used to route the data for the specific application that's waiting for it. So every host connected to the internet has a unique IP address, including yours. Now to find out what your IP address is, you can run a command from your operating system's command line but it's also often just as easy just to do a search for what is my IP. So if we do that and do a search for what is my ip. Now I'm going to block my public IP address so you can't see it, but that's a way to find out what the IP address is on your computer.

And you can also do a similar search on Bing and other search engines. Now the four numbers that will come back are in the form x dot x dot x dot x or you might also see a series of eight segments separated by colons. And that's because there are ipv4 addresses and ipv6 addresses. Now ipv4 stands for internet protocol version 4 and ipv6 stands for internet protocol version 6. So once upon a time there are only ipv4 addresses. Now ipv4 uses a 32-bit address scheme that allows for over 4 billion unique addresses.

But now that we've got computers, tablets, game consoles, smart tvs, smartphones, smart appliances etc. now that we've got those all connected to the internet and each device has to have a unique IP address. As a result, 4 billion IP addresses wasn't really enough and so ipv6 was born. Now it actually uses a 128 bit address scheme which allows for many, many more IP addresses than ipv4 does. Now ipv4 addresses are written as four integers separated by dots, and I'm sure you've seen that probably before but ipv6 addresses are written in hexadecimal and separated by colons.

But right now, we're in a transition period. So when you ask for IP addresses you may see the ipv4 address returned or you may actually see the ipv6 address. And while we're here IP stands for internet protocol. Now you may you may have heard the term TCP IP. Now that refers to using the TCP protocol with iep addresses and it doesn't necessarily mean the host is connected to the internet. Two applications running on the same host can use TCP to communicate with each other.

Now when the client and server are on the same host, usually the IP address 127.0.0.1 which is also referred to as localhost is used to identify the host So with that brief introduction to networking terms out of the way, let's actually start our tour of the java.net package. So the package contains two sets of APIs. Firstly, the low-level API and then the high-level API. Now when using the low-level API, you have to be more aware of networking concepts.

Still, when using java to do network coding, you're always working with abstractions regardless of whether you're using the high- or low-level API. Java actually makes network coding much easier than it could have been by letting developers write code using abstract concepts and taking care of the implementation details under the hood. Now because it's so common, we're going to use client server examples in these networking videos in this section.

Now you'll often want a reliable two-way communication link between the client and the server. This is where the TCP protocol comes in. Now TCP, which stands for transmission control protocol, establishes a two-way connection between hosts. And this connection is reliable in the sense that the two hosts talk to each other. When used with internet addresses, you get TCP which uses the client server model. So when communicating using TCP, the sequence of events are as follows.

Firstly, the client opens the connection to the server. Secondly, the client sends a request to the server. Third, the server sends a response back to the client. And step four, the client closes the connection to the server. Now steps two and three may be repeated multiple times before the connections closed. Now when using the low-level networking API, you'll use sockets to establish connections, send requests and receive responses. Now a socket is one end point of the two-way connection.

The client will have a socket and the server will have a socket. Now when you have multiple clients connecting to the same server, they'll use the same port. But each client will have its own socket. Now you'll use the socket class for the client socket and the server socket class for the server socket. Now what's wonderful about java is that all you have to do is provide the IP address and port when you create the socket you don't have to understand how TCP IP works.

So underneath the cover specific messages have to be sent to establish a connection between the client and a server, and this is a process that's called handshaking and the data has to be sent as packets which must be in a specific format. But you don't have to take a course in computer networking when you write network code using java. That's because it takes care of all these details under the covers. Now since we're talking about networking, we're going to have to write two applications to demonstrate how to do network coding.

. So one application will be the server and the other will be the client. So in the next video, we're going to start by writing a server application that just echoes back to the client whatever text the client sends to it. So I'll see you in the next video.

LECTURE 43.5: UDP Server and Client
----------------------------------------

All Right. So we finished our discussion on TCP in the last video. Now it's time to take a look at another protocol, UDP. And that stands for User Datagram Protocol. Now when using TCP, some handshaking has to take place between the server and the client. So in other words the client has to connect to the server, and the server has to accept that connection. So the client sends a request and the server sends a response. So it's a two-way connection, and there's tight coupling between the client and the server.

Now the TCP protocol also performs error checking and will resend messages that don't make it to the server. So it's quite a reliable protocol, but that reliability requires overhead which can ultimately affect performance. Now when using UDP, there's no handshaking at all. And the destination host which may or may not be a server doesn't actually send any responses to the message sender. So you use it when you don't need a reliable connection or a two-way connection or when speed is essential.

So if you require a response to a message you send over the network, then you wouldn't use UDP. So UDP uses datagrams. And a datagram is a self-contained message and is not guaranteed to arrive at its destination. Now UDP is often used for time-sensitive communication and when losing the odd message or packet here and there won't matter. For example, voiceover IP applications like skype and video streaming usually use UDP because speed is more important than ensuring that absolutely every package arrives.

Our eyes won't notice if the occasional package isn't received, for example, when we're watching a video. Also, the data arriving at the client is immediately replaced by more data, so it's not critical that all the messages reach the client. As mentioned, UDP is used for time-sensitive communication because the overhead involved with TCP is actually significant and so data can be sent much more quickly using UDP. So as usual, which protocol to use will depend on the application that you're looking to write.

So we're going to rewrite the clients and the server applications to use UDP. And you can see that I've actually created two new projects here. I've got a UDP server project on the left and the UDP client project on the right. So starting with a fresh base basically. And we're not going to worry about using threads this time since you now know how to do that from the TCP code that we worked on. And for this demo app, I just want to show how to send data using a datagram.

In a real-world application, you would definitely want to use threads like we did in the last few videos. All right. So let's start with the server side of things. You'd think that this would be an easy question to answer, but it's not necessarily that easy. So we just bring up a web page and paste in this link. So if you have a look here, you see there's a whole paper quite a detailed paper as I scroll down the screen there from the w3c.

That's the world wide web consortium by the way, responsible for web standards this entire paper is trying to explain the difference between a URL and a URI. So a good section to start with would be this section here under confusion. The body of documents RFIs etc. recovering URI architecture syntax registration etc. spans both the classical and contemporary periods. And the people who are well-versed in URI matters tend to use URL in URI in ways that seem to be interchangeable.

So among these experts, this isn't a problem but among the internet community at large it is. So people are not convinced that URI and URL mean the same thing in documents where they apparently do. So when one sees an RFC, by the way, an RFC's request for comments by the way it's a formal document from the internet engineering task force. So when 1 sees an RFC that talks about URI schemes another that talks about URL schemes and yet another talks about your n schemes, it's probably pretty natural to wonder what the difference is and how they relate to each other.

So can be a bit confusing, but with that as an aside let's stick to what we need to know to write java networking code. Now when working with a java.net package, a URI is an identifier that might not provide enough information to access the resource that it identifies. Now a URL, one on the other hand, is an identifier that includes information about how to access the resource that it identifies. So another way to state this is that a URI can specify a relative path but a URL has to be an absolute path. Because when we use the URL, it has to contain enough information to locate and access the resource that it identifies.

Now it's actually easy to convert between URLs and URIs. So all you really have to do is provide what the method you want to use requires, a URL or URI and you'll actually be fine. Now the recommended practice when working with the java.net classes is to use a URI until you actually want to access a resource and then to convert the URI to a URL. So having said that sometimes there's no need to start with a URI because the method you use to open or access a resource accepts a URL right off the bat.

Now I know that sounds terribly confusing, but let's see if we can make a bit more sense of this. So a scheme is part of a URI or URL that appears before the colon. So at this point you've seen how to use the http URL connection and URL collection classes to read web pages and retrieve specific data from web pages by passing parameters and that's actually great. But here's the thing to keep in mind. Many java developers don't use the classes in the java.net package when they want to work with URLs. So the java.net package has been in the JDK, all the way back since java 1.0.

And unfortunately, it really hasn't changed much since. Then under the covers there's just an older version of the http protocol. The classes that use the newer http 2.0 protocol were proposed and worked on for java 9 and the proposal listed the following problems as you can see on the screen, and I've taken this from the link you can see in the screen there openjdk.java.net jeps 110. So the problems that have found where the base URL connection API was designed with multiple protocols in mind nearly all of which are now defunct that's ftp gopher etc. The API predates http 1.1 and is too abstract as a result.

It's hard to use with many undocumented behaviors and it works in blocking modes only that is 1 thread per request or response and most importantly it's very hard to maintain. Unfortunately, the behavior of the java.net http classes can be frustrating, try setting parameters using the post method as in the sample code that I showed on the screen, and you could be tearing your hair out. That's because it doesn't always work. And when developers go to the web and try to find out why, other developers will usually say words the effect of don't use the java.net classes use a third-party library.

Now unfortunately, the proposed java 9 API has been placed in what's called the incubator, meaning that based on the feedback from developers who tried the early access java 9 features is not ready for prime time. So in other words, the API won't be in the base java 9 JDK, but developers will still be able to try it out by adding it to their projects. Now based on the feedback the API team expects to get from even more developers, the API may well be revised and then added to the JDK or it may also be deleted.

So it's not a good idea to use the new API in any applications you plan to release to users in the future. But in the meantime, many developers are using third-party libraries when they want to work with the http protocol. The 2 popular ones I want to talk about briefly are jetty and that's available from www.eclipse.org jetty and as well as the Apache http client hc.apache.org http components client - ga. Keep in mind that even though the Apache library only supports http 1.1, overall developers like it because it's much easier to use than the java.net classes.

So it's important that you've got a taste of the high level API though in the java.net classes so that you can read code that uses them. But when you want to work with the http protocol, you might want to consider using jetty or the Apache http client libraries.
